en: (?ṃ) Homage to the venerable Gurus;
homage to the venerable Sundaragaṇapati. [In the Vātula, the Chapter on Daily Worship] (re27521)
Om, Hari! I shall describe the worship based on latent impressions (vāsanā), which is meritorious, bestowing auspiciousness, destroying sins,
removing the defects of great transgressions, and granting the fruit of all sacrifices.
Worship is said to be of two kinds: for one's own sake and for the sake of others;
it is performed when the *liṅga* has been bestowed by the Guru, upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), or within oneself.
Sand, rice, river-clay, cow-dung,
fresh butter, a rudrākṣa, flour, sandalwood, and a brush.
Flower garlands, water, and ashes—these sixteen are the marks of the momentary;
worship for one's own sake is prescribed in a momentary mandala or in water.
The liṅga is said to be of six kinds: made of stone, made of gems, made of metal, made of wood, made of clay, and ephemeral.
For the sake of protecting all beings, especially in villages and other places,
a linga has been installed according to the prescribed rite by gods, sages, or men.
The self-arisen liṅga, which is the very essence of the Lord of the imageless, is declared to be for the sake of others; it is the fruit of the Self for all beings.
Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras who have been initiated are those who enter;
one should perform sacrifice for one's own sake, but not for the sake of another.
The Ādiśaiva must perform [rites] for his own sake and for the sake of others;
he is called Ādiśaiva because he is the teacher of Brahmā, who is together with Śiva.
Ādiśaiva, Śiva, Rudra, Śuddhātman, and Śuddhaśaivaka— therefore,
the Śaiva rite should be performed, beginning with the consecration and ending with the festival.
For the sake of one's own welfare and for the welfare of others, in the worship of the pure Śiva,
first there should be purification of the self, and secondly, purification of the site.
The third is the purification of substances, the fourth is the purification of mantras, and the fifth is the purification of the liṅga;
these are the five purifications.
Having performed his bath according to the prescribed rule, and thereafter having purified his body,
the wise man should wash his feet and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rule.
Facing north and seated upon a beautiful seat,
he assumed the lotus, the swastika, the cow-faced, and likewise twenty other postures.
The Sucīca, the Ekapāda, the Vīra-kukkuṭa,
as well as the Bhadrāsana, the Kūrma, and the Vimala should be known [as the postures].
The staff (daṇḍa), the ball (piṇḍa), the cow-ear (gokarṇa), and beyond that the lion-throne (siṃhāsana);
likewise the circle (vṛtta), the water-jar (ghaṭika), the elephant-mounted (gajastha), and the elephant-ear (gajakarṇika).
The seat is said to be of twenty types, the best being the firm and comfortable posture (sthira-sukhāsana).
In this, the two thighs, the two knees, and the tips of the feet are joined together in a hollowed enclosure.
With the gaze fixed on the tip of the nose, the body held straight and motionless—
this is declared to be the beautiful posture (rucirāsana), honored in all undertakings.
The cow-faced (gomukha), the auspicious cross-legged (svastika), the lotus (padma), the half-moon (ardhacandraka),
the heroic (vīra), and the yoga-posture (yogāsana) are thus declared to be the sixfold types of seats.
Having placed the right knee-circle upon the left knee,
one should place the soles of both feet on the sides and the back.
Having thus made the face of the cow (gomukha) very supple, it is known as the *lakṣaṇa* posture;
placing the thighs, sides, and soles [of the feet] together, this is here called the lotus posture (*padmāsana*).
Having placed the soles upon the thighs and sides, with the shanks submerged, it is the Svastika;
having placed the soles upon the thighs and the soles on both sides.
Having made the two ankles even, one should place the soles and the shanks together;
this is known as the Half-moon posture (ardhacandra). Now hear that Hero’s posture (vīrāsana).
With the right leg extended over the left and right [sides], it is called the firm Vīrāsana; now hear that Yogāsana.
The body, with the knees joined and covered by a yogic cloth (yogapaṭṭikā),
and with the forearms likewise placed [between them], is here called the yogic posture (yogāsana).
Having likewise prepared a seat made of kūrma-grass, darbha-grass,
and hide, he should then begin the purification of the directions by casting [offerings] toward the ten quarters with the Astra-mantra.
Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), each consisting of ten measures, the apāna sustains the prāṇa;
from the prāṇa, the Praṇava is said to emerge.
Through the union of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, it is called prāṇāyāma;
it consists of three parts: exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and the third, retention (kumbhaka).
Exhalation is declared to be *recaka*, inhalation likewise is *pūraka*, and retention by the cessation of both is *kumbhaka*; one should practice this triad with the *praṇava*.
Recaka has Brahmā as its presiding deity, pūraka has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity, and kumbhaka has Rudra as its presiding deity; these are proclaimed as the presiding deities.
The wise know that the syllables *a*, *u*, and *m* constitute the three-fold breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
The syllable *u*, which has the form of the moon, corresponds to the inhalation (*pūraka*) by the number of the sun.
The form of the letter *ma* is the sun, while the retention (*kumbhaka*) corresponds to the number sixteen;
the form of the letter *a* is fire, while the exhalation (*recaka*) corresponds to the number thirty-two.
First by means of the left channel, second by the right channel, and again third by the left; such is the sequence for performing breath control (prāṇāyāma).
One should exhale by pressing the nose while the wind is auspiciously in the abdomen;
then one should properly fill the belly with external air like a leather bag.
It is called Pūraketu; therefore it is termed Kumbhaka.
It neither grasps nor releases the breath situated within or without.
Therefore, because it is a "holding" (kumbha), it is called kumbhaka;
there has never been, nor will there ever be, a merit greater than prāṇāyāma.
The region from the feet up to the knees is said to be the station of earth;
the region up to the navel is the station of water, and the region up to the throat is the station of fire.
The station of air is at the forehead; twelve finger-breadths above that is said to be the station of space. These are the five stations beginning with the earth.
The forehead is one palm (tāla) in measure, and twelve finger-breadths (aṅgula) above that is declared to be the abode of Śiva; such is its measurement.
This secret Śiva-tattva is said to be the locus of space;
it consists of a square, a half-moon, a triangle, and a hexagon.
The earth and the other elements are well-rounded and circular in shape, respectively;
their colors are yellow, white, red, black, and smoke-colored.
Likewise, the letters *la*, *va*, *ra*, *ya*, and *ha* correspond to earth and the other elements;
the seed-syllables (*bīja*) correspond to earth and the other elements; and [these] are the five forms beginning with Brahmā.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara,
and Sadāśiva are declared to be the presiding deities (adhidevas) of the earth and the other elements, respectively.
The wise one should sequentially join the seed-syllables of earth and the other elements with the heart, head, crest, and armor mantras.
Five, four, three, two,
and one— by means of the Pāśupata scripture, one should dissolve these five knots.
Then, having made five knots from that [cord], one should determine the nature [of the body]:
the knee-knot is the first, and the navel-knot is the second.
The third is the throat-knot (galagranthi), while the fourth is on the forehead;
the fifth is the Brahma-knot—these five are known as the "five knots" (pañcagranthi).
The heart, the throat, the palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the Brahma-knot as the fifth;
or else, the five knots are prescribed in another manner.
Likewise, having severed the five knots, the self-yoke is prescribed;
with the Mūrtimantra, one should [place] the Jīva-hūṃkāra upon the heads.
It is declared that by means of the *kumbhaka* [retention], one should place [the breath] within the form of the wind;
by that very means, one should unite it with Śiva residing at the *dvādaśānta*.
Having thus performed its own conjunction, one should then purify the elements;
among earth and the others, water and fire should each be purified by the other in pairs.
Just as purity is described through space and light, so too are the elements beginning with Nivṛtti; these constitute the entire path.
One should consider these [elements] as existing pervasively and should purify them;
for living beings, burning and falling [into one another] constitute mutual purification.
The mandala and so forth have been fully described; now the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) is taught here [as follows]:
it is free from the taint of the objects to be purified and is established as mere time.
Having reflected upon the purpose of the divine body, one should lead [the breath] by means of immersion in nectar,
having meditated upon the Kuṇḍalinī power whose sole nature is nectar.

Having made that [deity] the seat within the heart— [the deity] which has become as if sprinkled by the flow of nectar arising from that [seat], and for which all latent impressions have been forgotten— one should perform the self-identification with its form.
Having performed the ritual immersion once more, one should perform the placement of the hands (karanyāsa).
Four finger-breadths below the navel is the circle of fire (agnimaṇḍala).
The second [cakra], located at the root of the navel, is said to consist of the mūlādhāra; it has the color of a kadamba flower, possesses eight petals, and is triangular in shape.
The great channel (nāḍī) shaped like a serpent’s coil,
a bracelet, or a circle is called the solar orb (bhānumaṇḍala).
Having grasped oneself with the withdrawal mudrā accompanied by the visualization of the form,
one should [dissolve] the fivefold self, beginning with the body, according to the prescribed rule and its proper measure.
The Self, the inner self, and the supreme self—
these are praised as the essential self, the self of gods and beings, and the self that has become all things.
The *ātman* is situated in the middle of the staff; the *antarātman* is within that;
the *paramātman* is situated in the lower part of that; and the *tattvātman* is on the right side.
The elemental self (bhūtātman) is said to be located on the left side of the body; it is the station of the fivefold self.
It is joined with the threefold self consisting of Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā in its state of stability.
The fivefold self is said to be the very locus; the son of the daughter (dauhitra) is in the middle of the sides.
The self is declared to consist of the qualities (guṇas), while the inner self (antarātman) is of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
Having meditated upon the Supreme Self, the one whose essence is reality perceives the face of the King;
likewise, desire for beings, ritual action, and even food arise.
The self, the soul of the elements, brings about the qualities of pleasure and pain, of conduct and renunciation, and of the other elements within living beings.
Thus, these have been declared as the self, which is difficult to attain at the times of worship;
they say that the letter *a* is the self, and the letter *m* is the inner self (*antarātman*).
The syllable *oṃ* is the Supreme Self; the syllable *u* is indeed the Self of reality;
and the syllable *e* is proclaimed as the Imperishable, the Self of all beings.
The wise Bhūtātman should join [the elements]; the Antarātman should burn them again;
the Tattvātman should fill them with nectar; and the Śuddhātman should bring them back once more.
One should unite [the soul] with the pure Śiva-tattva in the void at the tip of the crest-lock;
having done so, one should subsequently burn the body by means of that very [flame] which has gone to the triangle.
Beginning from the big toe, one should burn [the body] up to the head;
the body, enveloped in garlands of flames, becomes like a staff or a rope.
One should always contemplate the Praṇava as a white lotus, facing downwards, serving as the seat of yoga, from which the nectar that ends all worldly processes flows forth.
One should contemplate nectar within that [channel], with the *suṣumnā* piercing the skull;
then, one should meditate on oneself as being filled with that nectar.
The wise one should thus lead the self gradually toward Śiva,
[visualizing it] at the tip of the crest-lock twelve finger-breadths above, on both sides of the neck of the lute.
In the very center of the Suṣumnā is likewise a hollow space;
one should know Śiva to be in the Brahma-randhra. One should contemplate His dance above, for they know Him to exist as something exceedingly subtle beyond the Dvādaśānta.
The God of gods, the teacher of the world, is manifest as the dance of bliss;
he is the supreme beyond the supreme, in the form of a drop (*bindu*) between the white and the red.
Within that, the vital breath (prāṇa), consisting of the bindu and nāda, is Śiva.
Having made this distinction, listen now to another sequence.
On the back part of the anus, two finger-breadths above that,
there is a lotus with kadamba petals due to its connection with the neck of the lute (vīṇādaṇḍa).

In the Mūlādhāra and in the Smara [cakra], one should contemplate the fire of Śiva, which is joined with the moon and the sun; by virtue of its connection to the center of that, it is of the size of an atom.
Wind resides within form; mind resides within wind;
name resides within mind; and sound resides within name.
Śiva resides within sound; within sound resides Śiva.
Within Śiva is the Tranquil, which is beyond tranquility and higher than the highest.
"Beyond the beyond, the peaceful"—these [mantras] belong to the two states of Śiva.
First, however, is the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa), and after that, the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa).
One should purify the two palms and the backs of the hands with the weapon mantra;
one should purify the left hand twice with the weapon mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.
With the right hand, one should remember all the [deities] residing in the left hand;
having placed water in the left hand, the fire is situated in the right.
The placement of the fire-mantra (agnimāla) upon the [five] seats, accompanied by the ritual assignment of the hands (karanyāsa),
extending from the thumb to the little finger, is declared to be the "creation-assignment" (sṛṣṭinyāsa).
The placement [of mantras] starting from the little finger and ending with the thumb is called the *saṃhāra-nyāsa* (dissolution placement).
The placement starting from *Īśāna* and ending with *Sadyojāta* is declared to be the *sṛṣṭi-nyāsa* (creation placement).
The placement of dissolution (saṃhāranyāsa) is said to extend from Sadyojāta to Īśāna;
it begins with the right thumb and proceeds from the little finger to the others.
The wise one should place the ten seed-syllables; this is the supreme placement for stability (*sthitinyāsa*).
One should then place the limbs (*aṅga*) in sequence, beginning with the middle finger and ending with the index finger.
One should place the Eye on the palm of the hand and place the Weapon on the forefinger;
in this very manner, the limbs of Śiva are established at every joint.

A householder should perform the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) according to the path of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), whereas for forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) and ascetics (*yatīn*), it should indeed be performed according to the sequence of reabsorption (*saṃhāra*).
If one is without a wife, the *saṃhāra-nyāsa* (dissolution placement) is prescribed;
however, for a lifelong celibate (*naiṣṭhika*), the *sthiti-nyāsa* (maintenance placement) is honored in all ritual activities.

The ritual placement on the limbs (karanyāsa) has been fully explained; after this follows the ritual placement on the body parts (aṅganyāsa). Emission is said to begin from the head, while withdrawal should begin from the feet.
One should place Īśa on one's own head, and place Vaktra on the face;
having placed Ghora in the region of the heart, one should place Vāma in the secret organ.
One should place the *sadyojāta* mantra on the two feet, and then place the limbs;
having placed the heart-mantra on the heart, one should place the head-mantra on the head.
Having placed the *śikhā* [mantra] on the crest and the *kavaca* in the middle of the chest,
one should place the *netra* on the eye and the *astra* in the region of the hands;
thereafter, one should perform the placement of the thirty-eight *kalās* according to the prescribed rule.
Having cast off the ordinary state of being, one should contemplate, "I am Śiva.
Having done so, one should specifically perform the internal sacrifice (antaryāga).
Relying upon the navel-cakra, one should form the mandala of fire;
one should hold the moon in the heart and the mandala of the sun between the eyebrows.
One should perform the sacrifice in the heart, and one should conceive of Soma in the navel;
likewise, one should meditate upon the Lord, the omnipresent Master, in the middle of the eyebrows.
Having performed worship specifically by means of the path of the five obstructions,
one should constantly worship within the heart-lotus either three times or twice a day.
Alternatively, one may perform the sacrifice mentally at a single time;
this is declared to be the purification of the self. Now hear the purification of the place.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) one cubit in measure before Śiva,
he should then invoke the Earth, adorned with all her ornaments.
She has two arms and two eyes, is adorned with a crown and a casket,
wears a golden sacred thread, has yellow eyes, and is in the full bloom of youth.
Or one may meditate on Ambikā, who is yellow in luster, with a yellow face, eyes like the petals of a white lotus,
and hands joined in the gesture of reverence (añjali), holding a blue lotus.
Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings the Goddess of the Earth— who is beautiful in all her limbs— within his own heart by means of the mantra.
One should begin the clearing of the directions with the Astra-mantra alone;
this is declared to be the purification of the place (sthāna-śuddhi). Now, listen to the purification of the materials (dravya-śuddhi).
A shallow bowl, a vessel for water for the feet, a conch shell for water for sipping,
a water-jar, a vardhanī vessel, a flower-vessel, and a vessel for the arghya offering.

The wise one should wash [the eyes] with the Astra-mantra while gazing at them with the Hṛdaya-mantra; then, having enveloped them with the Kavaca-mantra, perform the opening of the eyes with that same mantra.
One should fill both the *vardhanī* vessel and the conch with auspicious water;
then, one should place the five Brahmans and the six limbs within the midst of that water.
Then, having performed [the preliminary rites] with the right hand, one should place the ten seed-syllables;
one should display the liṅga-mudrā and show the padma-mudrā.
Having sprinkled the vessels on all sides with water from the conch using the Vyāhṛtis,
[he should place] milk, curd, ghee, and so forth, as well as fragrance, flowers, and incense.
Taking this *vardhanī* vessel, one should sprinkle with water using the *puruṣa* mantra;
thus the purification of the materials is accomplished—now hear the purification of the *liṅga*.
Having paid homage to the God of gods, one should worship the deities of the door well;
one should worship Gaṇeśa above the threshold and on the right side.
He has the face of an elephant, three eyes, a dark complexion, and four arms;
in his left hands he holds a sweetmeat ball and an axe, and in his right hands a tusk and a rosary.
One should worship Sarasvatī on the left side of the Sun, adorned with all ornaments and wearing a sacred thread made of nāgas.
In the left hand, he should hold the gesture of granting fearlessness (*abhaya*) and the *gaṇḍikā*;
on the right, he should hold it joined with a lotus, or he may simply hold it.
One should perform external worship endowed with all the characteristics;
one should place Gaṇeśa above the feet and Śrī Devī to his left.
She has two arms and two eyes, is adorned with a jeweled crown,
possesses a yellow complexion, and is beautiful in all her limbs.
A lotus is in her right hand and a bilva fruit in her left hand;
the goddess is situated in the center of the lotus, with two hands on either side.
One should thoroughly worship the Śrī Devī, who is endowed with raised hands and a cloth, who holds the threefold sacrificial ladle for consecration, and who is joined by a white elephant.
On the right side of the serpent is Nandin, red in color,
with three eyes and four arms, endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons.
Holding a fierce tomara-weapon and a trident, and endowed with a rosary;
likewise, on his very left side, there is one with two eyes and two arms.
Gaṅgā is white in color and mounted upon a crocodile;
she holds a blue lotus in her right hand and a full water-pot in her left.
One should worship Nandin and Gaṅgā on the right side of the door, adorned with variegated garments and embellished with all ornaments.
And on the left side of the serpent is Mahākāla, black in color,
with four arms and three eyes; he holds a skull and a trident in his right hands, while his left hands are endowed with the gesture of fearlessness and a hammer.
One should represent him as endowed with matted locks and a crown, with a serpent serving as his sacred thread;
and on his right side, one should likewise depict the Yamunā.
Having two arms and two eyes, endowed with a dark complexion,
seated upon a tortoise, and adorned with all ornaments.
To the left of the full water-jar is an utpala lotus in her right hand;
she is Yamunā herself, beautiful in all her limbs.
On the left side of the door, one should worship Mahākāla and Yamunā;
and on his left, one should worship Yamunā and Mahākāla with great devotion.
One should worship Vimalā and Subāhu on the two door-panels;
having worshipped Skanda on the lintel, one should worship Sūrya and Soma on the two rings.
The ninefold power within the cavity shall proceed to the base of the weapons;
one should worship the Bull in front with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, in due order.
One should first worship the inner maṇḍala;
the second is the inner necklace, and the third is the middle necklace.
The fourth [circle] belongs to the Maryādīs, while the fifth is the Mahāmaryādī;
this is said to be the fivefold enclosure (pañcaprākāra), and one should perform the bali offering at each enclosure.
Whether at the entrance to the inner sanctum, or in a half-maṇḍapa,
or in a full maṇḍapa, [the installation] is classified as superior, middling, or inferior.
At that gate, one should visualize the gatekeeper, either seated or standing;
Dindiṇa on the right side and Muṇḍina on the left side.
Red in color, with two eyes, and having a serpent as his sacred thread;
of terrifying form, with prominent fangs, two arms, and one face.
One should meditate on the god Dindi, who possesses the form of a dwarf, standing at the left side, filled with wonder, with his hands joined together, and equipped with a staff as a weapon.
He is shaven-headed, black in color, with two arms and two eyes;
he is equipped with a staff as his weapon and adorned with serpent ornaments;
he possesses a hand-gesture of wonder, being shaven-headed in his true form.
When residing in the east, the guardian of that eastern gate should likewise face westward,
especially at the time of worship.
At the conclusion of the worship, having performed [the rites] as before, and likewise for the gatekeepers,
the wise one should strike the bell while reciting the weapon-mantra (astramantra).
At the time of worship, however, the striking of the bell serves the purpose of swift action;
likewise, it causes the asuras and rākṣasas to depart to a great distance.
At the invocation and at the conclusion of the worship, having offered the arghya, one should properly join [the offerings];
having bathed, one should properly join the arghya, the unguent, and the three fragrances.
During the consecration, the incense offering, the food offering, the ritual of oblations,
and the dismissal, one should strike the great bell.

At the time of performing rituals such as worship, one should avoid an excellent cloth that has been torn by those afflicted with sinful diseases, those who have fallen from their status, atheists, or revilers of Śiva.
The evil conduct of Durmukha, the reviler of his guru by the fool,
and the lack of devotion toward the Brahmins who have altered the Vedas and are devoid of bone [in their lineage].
The wheel and the syllable belong to one who has not been initiated;
for such a rogue, having entered and performed the visualization, it is fruitless if devoid of worship.
Having mentally envisioned the Concealed Cloth (pracchannapaṭa), which cuts through all defects,
and having removed the curtain while reciting the heart-mantra.
Then, having entered the inner sanctum (garbhageha), one should perform the purification of the Linga;
[namely] the self-manifested (svayambhu), the divine (daivika), the Bāṇa, the Gāṇapa, and likewise the Ārṣaka.
One should perform the worship of what is known as the *śiṣṭaliṅga* as previously described;
however, specifically regarding the *śiṣṭaliṅga*, there is no invocation (*āvāhana*) nor dismissal (*udvāsana*).
However, one should place that emblem which lacks the thread upon the head and in the center—
the God who pervades everywhere, the Supreme Lord Sadāśiva.
That which is the act of making [the deity] face toward oneself is called invocation (āvāhana);
that which is the act of turning [the deity] away is called dismissal (udvāsana).
But when the worship is completed, there is the dismissal of that [deity] who has turned away,
just as the fire situated in the sacrificial pit becomes kindled by the wind.
And likewise, by means of the linga alone, the Lord Śiva is born;
and by the gods and the sages, the multitude of bound souls (paśus) and the flocks of birds [are produced].
The Mṛgāṇāgas, the Āṇavas, and especially the Svayambhūs, as well as the Yakṣas, Rājas, and others— by them that liṅga was installed.
That which remains is called the *liṅga*, the cause for the presence of Śiva;
therefore, there is no invocation (*āvāhana*) nor any rite of dismissal (*udvāsana*).
Whence can there be an invocation of the deity, and whence, therefore, an dismissal here? They even forget the ritual dismissal of the gods and deities.
The invocation and the form of the Liṅga are traditionally known as the "Liṅgamūrti";
having performed these in the presence of the preceptor, one should gradually cover it with a mirror.
Just as thousands of lamps are not extinguished by the light of a single root lamp,
so too the worship of the deity in the *liṅga* does not diminish the singular root *liṅga*.
Just as milk, though originating as a single substance, takes on many colors when placed in various vessels,
so too is the one Lord manifested there in manifold forms.
Just as a potter is seen in various forms upon his wheel,
so too is the Supreme Lord perceived in many ways when one meditates upon the Teacher with the mind.
Wherever a deity is fashioned from stone, clay, wood, or paint,
that deity is surpassed by the Self-luminous One who is unfashioned.
Then, one should invoke the fire from wood, the moon from a jar, and the sun;
whatever deity one worships, that very deity shall become one's own self.
Uttering the Prāsāda mantra from the base (mūla) to the end of the twelve (dvādaśānta), the practitioner,
with palms joined in añjali, should apply it with fragrant flowers.
Through devotion, one has attained a state of equal flavor (*samarasībhāva*) that is partless and beyond the reach of the senses;
it is the end of power (*śakti*), the end of sound (*nāda*), the end of the partless (*niṣkala*), and the self-conquering peak (*kūṭasvajit*).
Having invoked the deity during meditation, listen now to that which is devoted to the perfuming of mantras:
O Vāsudeva, the nature of mantras is perfuming (*vāsanā*), and likewise, perfuming is their very nature.
But one who is naturally a carrier of burdens, like a horse that is both to be colored and born for it,
should not be yoked by the wise to what is neither to be yoked nor to be unyoked, nor to what is to be yoked and unyoked.
The abode of the intellects is in the heart; the heart is the abode of the physical body (piṇḍa). The abode of the bodies is the channel (nāḍī); the abode of the channels is the anus.
It is proclaimed as the abode of the winds, the abode of the powers, my own abode,
the abode of Śiva, and the abode of all mantras.
This is declared to be the dwelling of the mantra; it is called the invocation of the mantra.
[One should perform this] in the linga, the image, the water-pot, the site, and the fire at the root.
Furthermore, the invocation of the mantra is appropriate for the work of the potter (the ritual).
One should place the linga devoid of thread upon the head and in the center;
one should contemplate that cave as the face of the linga, according to its opening.
The face should be at the tip of the thread, the two arms at the sides of the thread, and the feet likewise at the end of the thread; thus, the back should be situated along the thread.
One should dismiss with the Īśāna mantra the flower worshipped during the previous meditation;
the wise practitioner should take hold of the flower with the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger.
One should cast away the flower by twirling it with the thumb and forefinger;
at the time of dismissal, one should cause that flower to be placed upon the heads [of the deities].
One should offer all remnants of the worship to Caṇḍeśa;
one should wash the liṅga with the Astra-mantra using the palm of the right hand.
One should wash the pedestal all around in sequence with the Pāśupata weapon-mantra;
then, having discarded the floral remains, one should wash the linga and the pedestal with water.
Purification and washing are proclaimed as the purification of the *liṅga*;
thus, there are twelve [purifications] for Śiva, and therefore this alone is its burden.
Its increase is recorded as one *bhāra* up to ten *bhāras*:
five *bhāras* in the forenoon and ten *bhāras* at midday.
Two bhāras at sunset, one and a half bhāras at the first twilight,
and eight bhāras at the final twilight— so it is remembered.
Listen to the enumeration of these substances for bathing:
cardamom, cloves, camphor, sandalwood, and agalloch wood.
Tatkola, kaccola, uśīra, campaka, and likewise harivera—
these are remembered as the bathing substances for all.
The height of the *liṅga* consists of four measurements:
one part is wrapped with a cloth, two parts are adorned with ornaments, and one part is beautified with flowers.
In one devoid of pride it causes a great disease, and in one who is superior it increases the enemy;
therefore, this ointment of all fragrances is said to be equal [to all].
One should cause the offering of mantra-flowers through the consecration with mantra-water;
the head and hands are always flowers, and flowers are the very form of the mantra.
The conjunction of mantras with fragrances is known as "mantra-flower" (mantrapuṣpa).
In this way, the purification of the liṅga is accomplished; now hear about the purification of the mantra.
The movement of the teeth and lips [is required] for the removal of impurity from the mantra;
indeed, the purification of the mantra is proclaimed by the utterance of the end of the *nāda*.
One should exhale by means of the upward stroke of the Suṣumnā channel, [expelling] the atoms that denote the deities, which are agitated by the *madhyeśa* (the central lord).

All mantras, especially those beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, should be employed in the ritual sacrifice; this is declared to be the purification of the mantra. He who knows these five purifications is worthy to perform the worship.
In performing a sacrifice during the transit of the sun or moon, one shall obtain that [result] as fruitless.
The worship that brings about the dissolution of the moon and sun is auspicious and bestows all accomplishments;
for the sun resides in the upward breath (prāṇa), while the moon resides in the downward breath (apāna).
One should effect the cessation of those two, which brings about the destruction of the moon and the sun;
having abandoned the night of lamps, how could the preceptor be worshipped?
The mind and the eye of all beings abide as the moon and the sun;
the mind is worshipped through the mind, not by one whose mind is elsewhere, for it is the very sight that honors the mind.
O Prajāpati, the eye is for the purpose of seeing;
as long as one has begun the act of worship, so long does the movement of the mind remain fixed upon the object of sight.
Having become intent upon no other gaze, and likewise devoted to the Supreme Single Syllable,
one should worship the Lord of Gods with that worship, and not otherwise than this.
O best of the twice-born, at whatever time one attains a state where the two— mind and eye—
are unified in a single-pointed mind, at that very time one should perform worship.
The time when the moon and sun perish is called *tatkāla*; at the moment of a solar transit (*saṅkrānti*) or an equinox (*viṣuva*), worship must never be performed.
The movement from one cavity to another cavity is called *saṅkrānti* (transition);
likewise, the hollow space situated between the two sides of the two cavities is also so designated.
The two, namely the mouth and the drinking vessel, are thus proclaimed as the Uneven (Viṣuma). One should perform the internal emission and worship that silence.
Standing at the southeast, one should worship that which is associated with the eastern gate;
one should likewise honor that which is associated with the southern gate, namely the southwest.
Standing at the one joined with the western gate, one should worship Nairṛta;
joined with the northern gate, one should worship the region of Vāyu.
One should worship facing north in the east and west;
and one should worship facing east in the north and south.
One should worship the deity while standing either before the fire or before Nirṛti,
using the waters from the ritual jar poured with both hands joined in the *saṃpuṭa* gesture.
Holding the water-pot with the downward-facing left hand,
[one should place it] at the tip of the bull-horn, measuring four finger-breadths at the top of the liṅga.
Having performed the consecration slowly while reciting the root mantra,
or else by another method, sequentially using cow's urine, water, and [cow dung].
With inhalations filled with water, with retention-locks (kumbhakas), with hand-retentions (pāṇikumbhakas),
and with exhalations of water, one should [apply them] slowly and in succession to the top of the linga.
The path of mantras, the path of words, the path of phonemes, and the cities;
the path of principles (tattvas) and the path of kalās—one should recite [the mantra] and worship the God.
Having uttered the Śiva-mantra while observing silence, one should perform the worship of Śiva;
then, in front of the front porch (or the eastern pavilion), [one should honor] the Brāhmaṇas who chant the Vedas.
One who has not been initiated, even if he is a knower of the four Vedas, should avoid touching the *liṅga*;
if one who is initiated lacks devotion, the kingdom and its ruler will perish.
Just as an elephant in the forest becomes terrified upon seeing the shadow of a lord of beasts,
so too does one incur fear upon seeing the deity without mantras and worship.
Born into a family of Śiva-brahmins and initiated into the Śiva-āgama,
he should worship the Lord of the gods according to the rites prescribed in the scriptures.
One should prepare a seat there, for the rite of worshiping Śiva is prescribed;
the support is called the seat, which Paramaśiva himself should fashion.
Nāda is known as the Liṅga, and Bindu is remembered as the Pīṭha;
there is no Śakti without Śiva, nor is there a Śiva devoid of Śakti.
Just as fragrance is to be known in flowers, and likewise oil in sesame seeds, so too is the power of the vital breath (prāṇa-śakti) within the body; therefore, the wise man should worship it.
Power alone is declared to be the seat; that is the fivefold seat in sequence:
Pārśva, Pāṇḍu, Skanda, Nāla, and Vahni—thus it is called.
Then, first is the Anantasana, the second is the Simhasana,
the third is the Yogasana, and the fourth is the Padmasana.
The fifth is indeed named Vimala; these [five] consist of the nature of the five elements.
It has the form of a circle, is infinite, and possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns.
One should visualize [the elements] below and fashion the lion-throne above;
[these represent] the fourfold set of dharma, jñāna, vairāgya, and aiśvarya.
White, ruby-red, golden, and with the luster of emerald—
these shall be the colors of the [deities] beginning with Dharma, in the sequence starting from the southeast (āgneya).
One should imagine lions in the forms of the four corners of the courtyard,
with faces formidable with fangs, possessing three eyes, and having the appearance of the earth.
Each one, moreover, has a retinue of ten million lions;
likewise, [they possess] unrighteousness, ignorance, lack of dispassion, and lack of sovereignty.
One should arrange all [the elements] resembling lapis lazuli in the directions starting with the east;
having thus struck them with the three qualities, the lion-throne (siṃhāsana) comes into being.
In the corners, in the form of spirits (bhūtas), are the pairs of feet and the beginnings of the ages;
their colors are white, red, black, and yellow, according to the sequence beginning with Ketu.
The fourfold [principles] are the Unmanifest, Necessity, Time, and Kalā.
The Unmanifest has the luster of crystal; Necessity has the brilliance of gold.

Kāla has the luster of a pomegranate flower; Kalā has the brilliance of split collyrium. These are said to be placed starting from the east [and proceeding clockwise]; Keśava, however, is in the middle square.
Thus yoga-posture has been described; above that is the lotus posture (padmāsana), which is the principle of Māyā, a great knot adorned with the lotus of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā).
One should arrange the petal-section of the Vidyeśvaras, covered and joined with the filaments of Śakti;
therein, one should fashion the pericarp consisting of the principle of Vidyā (vidyā-tattva).
The seed has the luster of a coral-colored gem, the sprout has the brilliance of silver,
its stalk is indeed of lapis lazuli, and the thorn is reddish-brown.
The tips of the petals are the color of a conch shell, while the lower parts of the petals are remembered as red; the filaments in the center should be slightly reddish-yellow.
In the center of that, the wise one should fashion a pericarp with the luster of gold;
in the middle of that, he should fashion nine seeds with the brilliance of gold.
One should assign the eight powers, beginning with Vāmā, to the arrows;
one should place [the lords] from Indra up to Īśāna [in their respective directions], and Manonmanī in the center.
One should place the principle of the Self (ātmatattva) in the right [hand], the principle of Knowledge (vidyātattva) in the left,
and the knower of ritual procedures should conceive of the principle of Śiva (śivatattva) in the middle.
Thus the yogic posture (yogāsana) has been described; above that is the stainless seat (vimalāsana).
One should likewise arrange the triple mandala for the stainless seat.
The lion throne is four-cornered; the seat of Ananta is triangular;
the lotus seat is circular in shape; and the stainless seat (vimalāsana) is hexagonal.
One should prepare the yogāsana, which consists of eight parts;
for the yoga of invocation and the seat, the siṃhāsana should be used.
The worship is the great lotus of the lowest [grade], while the food is called Vimala;
the hymn of praise, the music, and the dance belong to Anantāsana itself.

In the forenoon one should wear white clothing, at midday red clothing, and in the evening yellow clothing; however, during the final three-hour period (sārdhayāma), one may wear any color whatsoever.
Through devotion, the practitioner attains the state of equal flavor (*samarasībhāva*) regarding the movement of the partless (*niṣkala*);
[he does so] by means of the sequence ending in *nāda*, as well as within the radiance of power (*śakti*), in *nāda*, and likewise in the *bindu*.
When the deity has emerged through the ray of power (śaktikiraṇa) in due sequence, that is the invocation (āvāhana).
Just as the embryo resides within the egg, so does Śiva reside within the liṅga.
The life-force residing within the mother’s womb, which is the full nature of the self,
becomes the presence of the partless Śiva through the yoga of devotion, mantra, and ritual action.
Having washed his hands and feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), the wise man should perform every rite with a pavitra-grass ring upon his hand.
If the tip is thick and it remains in the form of a neuter *itikā*, and the root is indeed thick, it is a woman; if it has a prominent tip along with a root and is putrid, it is declared to be a man.
The dark-complexioned one has ears reaching down to her collarbones, long and straight;
she is adorned with playful grace, like Viśvāmitra, Kuśa, Daśaratha, Kala-ma rice, Dūrvā grass, barley, and the sky.
Kuśa grass, kāśa grass, daśīra grass, dūrvā grass, as well as vrīhi rice, viśvāmitra, and barley— these are proclaimed to be the seven types of darbha.
One should join [the breath] with both hands and also with the ring finger.
One should perform the act of sipping water (ācamana) with the hand holding the purifier (pavitra);
however, the purifier does not become defiled by it, yet one must avoid that which is defiled by food.
The material for the guest-house [shrine] consists of five types, with a brush (*kūrca*) measuring eighteen finger-breadths;
the knot is two finger-breadths at the tip, and the brush is of three grades—superior, middling, and inferior—each being half that size.
With its tip pointing upward, it is said to bestow nourishment; with its tip pointing downward, it becomes pacificatory.
It should be thirty-two finger-breadths long, provided with two rings, and elevated at the shoulders by a blade of darbha grass.
The *ketudaṇḍa* (banner-staff) is seated upon the head; the *makula* (bud) is the tuft (*kūrca*) at the tip of the *śrātā* (the cord);
the *kilapañcaka* (five spikes) resides in the jar (*kumbha*); the *staraṇaka* (spreading cloth) is the seventh; and the ninth is the *hivāva*.
One should likewise mutter the "grasping" mantra consisting of the three blades of grass called *jñāna* and the six [fingers];
this is declared to be the characteristic of the sacred thread (*pavitra*). Now hear the characteristic of the lower garment (*paridhī*).
The thick, rope-like [limb] resembling a finger, dark and mounted, is neither a plaything nor a bite; it is auspicious, like an arm with its upper part.
Thus, having properly encircled the enclosure with a wall, one should prepare twelve finger-breadths of fuel-sticks for the purpose of the fire-oblation, shaped like a staff to be held in the hand.
The characteristics of the enclosing sticks (paridhi) have been declared; hereafter follows the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna).
Cow dung from a Kapila cow is best, while that from a white cow is middling.
One who is red or black and of the lowest caste should take [the materials] upon a lotus leaf;
with the *sadyojāta* mantra one should take the cow-dung, and with the *vāmadeva* mantra one should form the lump.
The most excellent preceptor should indeed cause it to be dried with the Aghora-weapon mantra;
once burnt with the Śiva-mantra, he should then cause it to be taken up with the Tatpuruṣa-mantra.
The practitioner should place it in a gourd vessel or keep it in ashes;
having placed it in a new earthen jar, it should be protected by the *kavaca* mantra.
One should recite the Pañcabrahma-mantra together with the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) once over the Vyomavyāpin;
then, with the right hand alone, one should place it upon the left hand.
Having performed [the rites] beginning with gazing, one should deposit the five Brahma-kalās:
the head is smeared with the Īśāna-mantra, and the face with the Tatpuruṣa-mantra.
Having smeared the heart, the arms, the shanks, the navel, the back, and the chest with the Aghora mantra, one should then smear them with the Vāmadeva mantra.
The triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is made with the middle, ring, and index fingers;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the presiding deities of the triple mark.
The creation, maintenance, and dissolution [of the universe] are represented by the three lines of the Tripuṇḍra;
it should be worn during the forenoon, at meals, during ritual sipping, and even while lying down.
The ash-bath and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) are prescribed as providing all-encompassing protection;
they bring prosperity, are purifying, and ward off grief and disease.
This ash brings mastery over the world, is meritorious, and is the means for accomplishing the three worlds;
it is Brahmā himself when placed on the head, and Skanda himself when on the forehead.
In both ears, Śrī and Bhūmi are the presiding deities;
in the ear, Vināyaka and Prīti, and likewise Keśava in the two arms.
Īśvara is in the heart, Prajāpati in the navel,
and likewise Durgā, Sarasvatī, and Skanda in the back.
The Jahnu river and the Aśvins reside in the feet, as does the serpent;
whatever merit is found in all sacred fords (tīrthas) and whatever fruit is obtained from all sacrifices,
multiplied by ten million times ten million, one is purified by the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna).
For all members of the four castes— whether women, men, or eunuchs—
it may be performed three times a day, twice a day, or even once a day.
It provides protection for all beings and leads them to the world of Śiva,
having performed [the rite] in the presence of Śiva, the sacrificial fire, and the guru.
One must perform the smearing with ashes; one must perform purification upon the ground for as many particles of ash as fall upon the earth.
For as many thousands of yugas as there are grains of ash that have fallen on the ground through negligence and have been wiped away by the hand, the one who performed that act shall go to hell.
Having touched the head with the *rasanā* and *suṣumnā* channels, one should then meditate upon Śiva;
for Brahmins, [the distance] is six finger-breadths, and for Kṣatriyas, four finger-breadths.
The triple mark (tripuṇḍra) of three finger-breadths grants all desires for Vaiśyas;
that of one finger-breadth is for Śūdras and likewise for women.
Then the wise one [declared] that this is the destroyer of all sins;
it is effective even upon seeing bad dreams or touching wicked people,
and for a man who is unable to bathe, as well as for those who are always ill.
They are purified by bathing with ashes; you are worthy of being honored.
May the fever-demons, the *piśācas*, the *dhānakas*,
the spirits of Kumāra and Guha, the *kūṣmāṇḍas*, and even the *ḍākinīs* come forth.
Protection against the fear of tigers, serpents, and nāgas is provided by all [these means]:
the bilva fruit in the form of a liṅga, and likewise the leaf of the bamboo.
By the written command of Śambhu, one should likewise [avoid] the Aśvattha and Udumbara trees when they are broken apart,
when being consumed, when being shaved, and when plunging into water.
Having touched a eunuch or a woman, one should perform the purificatory bath prescribed by Agni;
furthermore, one should apply the circular *puṇḍra* mark beginning with thirty finger-breadths in width.
The trident, the half-moon, and the lamp—these five [ornaments] are placed in succession:
above the eye on the forehead is the staff, and the headband is bound around it.
The *tripuṇḍra* on the eastern face is circular with its tip pointing upward;
on the southern face it is a trident, and on the western face it is a half-moon.
In the northern face, the six-faced one is said to have the form of a lamp;
situated in the middle of the forehead-eye, its purpose is the power of protection.
The fire, having received the oblation of all substances, should be conceived as being free from defects;
[one should apply] four-finger-length [lines] on the forehead, the heart, and the two arms.
Having applied the *tripuṇḍra* in this manner with pure and skillful fingers—
after sleeping, rising, reciting prayers, and performing the necessary duties— one is purified.
At the conclusion of each watch of the day, one should perform an ash-bath;
likewise, one should avoid contact with crows, vultures, dogs, and those of other castes.
A heap of corpses, a cremation ground, a village of camels, pigs, and chickens; those who eat discarded offerings, ghosts, spirits, and the fallen—all these together [constitute the assembly].
Likewise, one should perform the Varuṇa bath even with other sectarian marks;
for even after performing a hundred water baths and a thousand mantra baths, [the true purification remains].
Merely by the smearing of ashes, Rudra is seen with affection;
[he looks upon] those whose bodies are smeared with ashes from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.
The *liṅga* that exists everywhere is called that god Śiva;
when protected on all sides, even deadly poison is thus destroyed.
Therefore, it is proclaimed as "Rakṣā" (Protection), which bestows the hand of Śiva;
it is the prosperity that brings prosperity to men, and the supreme protection that acts as a guardian.
It is called *bhasita*, spoken of as *bhāsita*, and declared to be *bhasma* because it consumes all impurities;
just as fire rests within ashes, [all things] have gone to dissolution in that very [Brahman].
Through the ash-bath, one becomes radiant and appears like fire;
a learned Brāhmaṇa should not transgress the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), even in his thoughts.
Since it is prescribed after being heard, one who abandons it becomes fallen.
May this ash, smeared upon my ears and used for smearing the body, become pure for me; through its purification, may the goal of liberation, whose nature is bliss, be attained.
These are those very ashes, purified by the mantras of Śiva, which serve as ornaments for the limbs that consume all desires.
The silver marks of the triple-line (tripuṇḍra) shining upon the forehead are like ill-written letters inscribed by fate.
If a practitioner who performs the worship of Śiva does not wear rudrākṣa beads,
that act is declared to be as fruitless for him as an oblation poured into the fire with mere ashes.
Whoever wears Rudrākṣa beads becomes Rudra himself; of this there is no doubt.
Even a dog is saved if it merely touches a clay image of Rudrākṣa.
Even he attains the state of Rudra; how much more so then humans and others?
He by whom a garland of eight hundred Rudrākṣas is fashioned and constantly worn on the ear—oh, by him the merit arising from [the gift of] a horse, a chariot, and so forth is obtained in an instant!

O Hāhā, the Gaṇa Navadya, when he carried loads of Rudrākṣas at the tip of the spear, he became a corpse and a donkey; yet on Kailāsa, for a period equal to a hundred crore kalpas, he was [reborn as] such.
If ash has been placed in the hand of a Śūdra, one should not wear it;
if one wears it out of delusion, he should perform a bath with water.
This ash-bath is eternally purifying, constantly cleansing, a destroyer of disease, and leads to excellent liberation;
it is equal to the holy ford of the Gaṅgā, a remover of all poisons, a pacifier of anger, and most tranquil.
It removes the powerful pride of Yakṣas, Piśācas, and Rākṣasas, and bestows contentment, nourishment, and prosperity.
O Lord of Pārvatī, may the grace of the Mountain-Dweller bring happiness to all people and ensure the subjugation of men in this world.
The ash-bath is the supreme sacred site, eternally destroying all sins;
Śiva himself is manifest in the form of ash, and ash is the means for accomplishing the three worlds.
For the sake of protection, for the sake of auspiciousness, and for the sake of the Supreme Self and purification,
one should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with white ashes during the three junctions of the day.
Freed from all sins, one is glorified in the world of Śiva;
this is declared to be the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna), and one should perform the bath of Mahendra.
When it rains or will rain, one should look at the hands and shoulders while facing east;
neither with arms raised nor with the left hand placed upon the right.
One should recite the root mantra with the voice seven times;
then, after [reciting] "Ādityādimukha," one should likewise say "tannamaḥ."
By doing this, one is liberated from great sins; there is no doubt about this.
This is called the Māhendra bath; now hear about the Māruta bath.
In the forenoon or in the afternoon, having been sprinkled with dust from the hooves of a cow while recollecting the root mantra, O practitioner of mantras.
At the conclusion of that, having performed the mantra-bath and having washed one's hands and feet,
and having rinsed the hands and sipped water (ācamana), one should likewise pour the water into a vessel.
The Guru, having consecrated that water once with the *vyomavyāpin* mantra, the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), the five Brahmans, and the root mantra (*mūla*).
One should touch [the body] with that water using the root mantra and the armor mantra;
likewise, one should perform the touching three times from the head down to the feet.
It liberates one from all sins and destroys all diseases;
it is known by the names of the mantras Vāruṇa, Māhendra, and Māruta.
Thus, this fivefold ablution is honored in all rites.
Having fully described the fivefold bath, now hear the procedure for the water for the feet and the other offerings.
Saffron, sandalwood, dūrvā grass, uśīra, and white mustard,
combined with a ploughshare, is declared to be the most excellent water for the feet (pādya).
Uśīra, sandalwood, dūrvā grass, and white mustard seeds,
combined with water, are said to constitute the middle-grade water for washing the feet (pādya).
Water mixed with sandalwood and uśīra is called the lowest grade of water for washing the feet;
holding each [ingredient] individually is best, while half of that amount would be middling.
Half of that is to be known as the lowest; this is remembered as the measure for the materials of the *pādya*.
The *pādya* water is offered once to each foot, beginning with the right foot.
The substances known as *pādya* (water for the feet) have been described; now hear the substances for *ācamana* (water for sipping):
*uśīra*, nutmeg, camphor, *tuṭi*, *trijātaka*, and cloves.
The supreme water for sipping (ācamanīya), combined with water,
is joined with cardamom, cloves, camphor, usīra, and jasmine.
That which is joined with water alone is remembered as the *madhyama* sipping;
that which contains cardamom, cloves, and ashes is remembered as the *kanyasa* sipping.
One should determine their measurements as before;
one should offer water for sipping at the mouths with an unbroken stream of water.
The substance for the sipping of water (ācamana) has been declared; now hear concerning the substances for the respectful offering (arghya):
nut-grass (mustā), fresh butter, the tips of kuśa grass, and white mustard seeds.
Camphor, *laghupatra*, and clove are said to be the eighth;
this is known as the *arghya* substance, which one should place upon the head at the time of worship.
Water with the tips of kuśa grass, unbroken grains of barley and rice, sesame seeds, and white mustard— this is called the supreme *arghya*.
An offering of barley, mustard seeds, rice, and so forth, with rice grains, is the middling *arghya*; water with rice grains of the *śāli* variety is the lowest *arghya*.
One should determine the quantity of the materials for the *arghya* offering as before;
the materials for the *arghya* have thus been fully described—now hear concerning the materials for the bath (*snāna*).
Water originating from the Gaṅgā and other rivers, or that which arises from lotus ponds,
fragrant with flowers, and filled in a new earthen jar.
The son of Śuddhavastra was pure and endowed with the fragrance of cardamom and other spices;
he was joined with the scent of cardamom, vetiver, the three fruits, myrobalan, sugar, camphor, fine saffron, divine sandalwood, agallochum, cinnamon leaves, and flowers.
Just as water is employed in the rite of purification for Śambhu according to availability,
so too among the substances mentioned here, that which is obtained from among those to be accepted should be taken by others according to their qualities.
Sandalwood, nutmeg, and camphor—this collection arises from the *aśira* tree;
having carefully placed a *niṣka* weight of these into water, one should immerse them in the waters with diligence.
Having covered it according to the prescribed rite, one should cause it to be placed within a hidden golden vessel;
then, taking a droṇa of water, [one should use] water purified by a cloth.
A bath with eight *droṇas* of water is declared to be the smallest;
the middling is known to be double that, and the best should be triple.
From one *bhāra* up to nine *bhāras*, there are nine types of liṅgas, ranging from the lowest to the highest;
even a single *bhāra* may increase according to the number nine as it has been proclaimed.
It should be known as "auspicious water" (śivāmbhas), consecrated with the Śiva-mantra;
it contains the four aromatics (cāturjāta), takkola, uśīra, and jasmine flowers (jātipuṣpa).
Thus, these seven substances are known as the five substances;
they are celebrated as the materials for bathing, and now the characteristics of the cloth are described.
Garments that are very variegated, substantial, and soft;
(and likewise tamukkāla, kaccola, uśīra, campaka, and haribera— these five substances are traditionally prescribed for all.)
The sacrificial posts (yūpa) should be well-adorned with flowers, fresh, and stripped of their bark;
they should be bound with golden threads, woolen cords, cotton strings, or fine silk cloth.
That which is endowed with a proportion suitable for divine ornaments is declared the supreme form of the deity's body; that which is of medium size is called the kṣoma.
A garment made of cotton threads is considered inferior;
that which measures sixteen cubits is superior, and twelve cubits would be middling.
One should conceive of three types:
the lowest should be nine cubits, the highest should be nine cubits, and the middling should be seven cubits.
The lowest [quality] cloth shall measure five cubits; this is declared to be the characteristic of cloth, according to the prescribed measurement of its threads.
For that many thousands of yugas, he is honored in the world of Śiva;
[if it is] black, there will be loss of position; and if killed, it causes harm to the king.
The appearance [of these signs] indicates the destruction of the village and the ill-omened ruin of the kingdom;
the characteristics of clothing have been explained, and now the characteristics of fragrance are being described.
Camphor, saffron, tamāla leaves, the sword, and the three fruits, along with sandalwood, uśīra, and iron— these are said to constitute the supreme fragrance.
Uśīra, sandalwood, camphor, the three fruits,
and nutmeg combined together are called the "medium" incense.
Hima, ghana, and karpūra are said to be the inferior (kanyasa) fragrances;
divine pratiphala is the best (śreṣṭha), while half of that would be the middling (madhyama).
Half of that is to be known as the lowest; such is the proclaimed nature of fragrance.
This is celebrated as the substance of fragrance; now the characteristics of the conch are being stated.
Highly refined silver and copper, and especially a vessel of bell-metal—
these, when compared with leaves of the *palāśa* or lotus, are equal to a copper vessel.
The conch should be known as fourfold, according to the sequence beginning with the Brāhmaṇa:
it is light and possesses a beautiful nature, with a long tip and a smooth back.
A Brahmin whose belly is full is called a Śaṅkha;
he has a long, straight tail, is graceful, and shines like gold.
A conch with a clockwise whorl is said to belong to a Kṣatriya;
it is slightly yellow in color and possesses a leftward turn.
That which is heavy, light, and even is known as the Vaiśya conch;
that which belongs to the Śūdra caste is light, with a long tip and a short back.
Relying slightly on the black [line], it is remembered as the "Śūdra-Śaṅkha.
Between the Gaṅgā and the ocean, between the Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya Śaṅkhas;
and between the Narmadā and the Sindhu, between the Vaiśya and Śūdra Śaṅkhas.
One should give a full handful [of water] to all; this is called the clockwise circumambulation of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
The front is said to consist of Viṣṇu; the belly is Gaṅgā and Sarasvatī;
the back is known as Prajāpati; and the two sides are the Aśvin deities.
One should hold the conch for the preceptor while recollecting the Śakti-mantra, [thinking]: "The god Candra, the Ṛṣi Candra, Sāvitrī, and Aṅgiras."
The characteristics of the conch have been declared; now hear about the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Milk is in the center; curds are in the direction of Indra (the east);
ghee is in the direction of Yama (the south); and two [products], cow dung and urine, are in the direction of Varuṇa (the west), the quarter of the Moon.
One should place the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in the southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast corners, having ground them with water mixed with clay.
In the nine squares on the right, one should place Sādākhya and Vidya; then, in the six compartments designated as Puruṣa and Prakṛti, one should subsequently arrange Supratiṣṭhā,
Suśānta, Tejas, Rūpa, Ratna, Udaka, and Amṛta within those vessels of the Unmanifest (Avyakta).
Milk, curd, clarified butter, cow urine, cow dung, and water with kuśa grass.

The wise one [should offer] red chalk, speech, the water for the feet, Śiva, Sadāśiva, the principle of the Person (puruṣatattva), that which is called Time (kāla), Niyati, Kalā, Rāga, Vidyā, and the Treasury of Knowledge (vidyākoṣṭha).
One should employ the bowls as follows: Supratiṣṭha, Suśāntā, Tejovat, Ratnaja, Hṛdā, Amṛtā, and Vyaktapātra.
The best of instructors should cause four threads to be laid out with their tips pointing eastward, and likewise four threads pointing northward, each measuring one *tāla* in length.
For the *śāla* tree, one *māḍhaka* is prescribed; three *prasthas* would be the medium size, and two *prasthas* should be known as the smallest, for each of the jars individually.
One should adorn it with half as much rice, and with half as much sesame seeds again,
and especially with parched grain, darbha grass, flowers, and fried grains.
One should wrap all the jars, which are endowed with auspicious marks and filled with four prasthas [of grain], with thread at intervals resembling lattice windows.
Rice has Brahmā as its presiding deity; Darbha grass has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity;
and the thread has Īśvara as its presiding deity—thus the presiding deities are proclaimed.
The ghee of a tawny cow is the best; the milk of a black cow is excellent;
curd from a white cow is preeminent, as is the urine of a red cow.
It resembles a fish-bowl and causes what was spoken once to fall away;
thus indeed is the acquisition of the cow, whether it be white or black.
At the time of the viewing, with a serene mind, one should take cow-dung along with its calf;
having taken it in hand, it is auspicious when it does not fall upon the ground.
One should diligently collect the milk that has been freshly drawn from the udder; without curdling it, one should take the curd with great care and firmness.
Clarified butter is for Kāśyapa; likewise, curd is said to be for Kauśika;
milk is for Bhāradvāja, and cow dung is for Gautama.
Agastya and Gomūtra are proclaimed as the sages (ṛṣis);
ghee has Rudra as its deity, and curd has Soma as its deity.
Milk has Śukra as its presiding deity, cow dung has Arka as its presiding deity, and cow urine is from the Gaṅgā;
these are the presiding deities of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
The highest [measure] is thus one *droṇa*, the middle is half of that, and the lowest should be known as half of that; one should thus determine the three types.
Clarified butter is indeed one *prastha*, curd is two *prasthas*,
milk is said to be three *prasthas*, and cow dung is four *prasthas*.
Six *prasthas* of cow urine is indeed praised as the best;
one should especially worship [the faces] beginning with Īśāna and ending with Sadyojāta.
Milk, adorned by one, two, three, four, five, or six monks, wards off enemies; curd bestows sons; ghee grants liberation and destroys sin;
cow dung brings all auspiciousness; and cow urine, along with the water from the stream, brings welfare.
This water from the tip of a blade of kuśa grass, when combined with fragrance, bestows all benefits;
it grants satisfaction for hunger and wind, provides nourishment, and brings delight. For those who sacrifice, bathing and other such acts constitute the threefold merit.
Milk shall bring about the destruction of enemies; curd leads to the increase of sons;
ghee bestows liberation, and cow’s urine brings about prosperity.
Cow dung shall be the destroyer of sin; it shall yield the fruit of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
These are cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with kuśa grass.
Known as Brahmakūrca, one should perform an ablution at the time of worship;
it is called Pañcagavya, and now hear about Pañcamṛta.

Having duly established the *mantra* at the vulnerable point (*randhrapada*), one should worship the Moon in the vessel of milk; Indra [should be worshipped] in the curd, the Sun in the vessel filled with clarified butter, and Soma in the vessel of honey.
Afterwards, one should likewise worship Varuṇa in the purified sugar, Fire in the vessel of *dhātrī*, and likewise [the others].
One should likewise consume flour, wind, and water with *kuśa* grass every night for the sake of Śambhu.
Milk, curd, ghee, sugar, and honey constitute the fivefold [offering];
likewise, honey, milk, white [sugar], clarified butter, and the essence of sugarcane, each individually.
Milk, curd, ghee, honey, sugar, and so forth, in their proper order;
likewise, the essence of fruit, the essence of sugarcane, and the essence of flowers.
Coconut oil and the five nectars (pañcamṛta) are mentioned here;
one should worship this Brahma-pañcāmṛta with the Sūkta mantras.
This is declared to be the five nectars (pañcāmṛta); one should worship the limbs of Brahmā [with them], with each measure being a full *prastha*, while the middling measure is half of that.
Half of that is to be known as the lowest; here, the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) are spoken of.
These five and these five constitute the various individual consecrations.
The consecration (abhiṣeka) should be performed with the five Brahmans, beginning with Sadyojāta;
[the practitioner] is honored in the world of Śiva for thousands of millions of kalpas.
One should bathe the Lord of the Gods with curd, milk, and likewise with ghee;
with coconut water and ghee, with honey, and with the five products of the cow.
This is declared to be the five nectars (pañcāmṛta); now hear the ritual services (upacāra).
The wise one should offer water for the feet (pādya) to the two feet once at each foot.
One should offer water for sipping (ācamana) into the mouth with an uninterrupted stream of water;
then, having placed the water-offering (arghya) upon the head, one should apply fragrant unguents to the limbs.
Having placed the flower upon the heads, the incense in the nostrils of the Lord,
and having placed the lamp upon the eyes, one should place the food in the palms of the hands.

One should offer food to be chewed, food to be swallowed, drinks, and likewise items to be sucked or licked; then, having placed a flower in [the devotee's] hand, one should afterwards give water for sipping (ācamana).
The water for washing the feet has the Earth as its deity; the water for sipping has Sarasvatī as its deity;
the water for the guest-offering (arghya) has the goddess Śrī as its deity; and the fragrance indeed has Vāyu as its deity.
The wise man should contemplate that the flower has the Gandharvas as its deity, the incense has the Moon as its deity,
and the lamp has the Sun as its deity for all of them.
One should offer [the water] to all the deities with the left hand;
the *pādya* (water for the feet) destroys sins, while the *ācamanīya* (water for sipping) brings prosperity.
The *arghya* offering brings success to one's actions; *gandha* becomes Govardhana;
flowers are said to bestow nourishment; and the offering of incense grants purification.
The lamp is said to bring subjugation, while the *ārātrika* rite bestows victory;
the sacred ash is for the protection of the universe, and especially for the king.
The mirror is said to bestow knowledge; the umbrella is the protection of wisdom;
the fly-whisk shall be the destruction of enemies; and song and instrumental music grant happiness.
There should be no withholding of grain; let there be an increase in food, for water is the protector of life.
For the sake of creation and the pacification of the planets, one should offer milk and other sweet substances.
By offering betel-leaf and flowers, one shall obtain happiness for the worlds;
bathing is for the destruction of disease, and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) remove impurity.
The gift of clothing here is said to bring about the creation of one’s own self;
likewise, by worshipping with articles of enjoyment, one shall obtain all enjoyments.
Through ornaments made of gold, gems, coral, and the like, there shall be the attainment of half the fruit; indeed, there shall be all prosperity and the pacification of all evil deeds.
There shall be fearlessness from all mantras regarding weapons such as the trident;
there shall be the destruction of disease, grief, and the like, and the total eradication of all poverty.
It causes the destruction of all enemies, the eradication of all calamities,
and brings peace to all men, and especially to the gods.
The rites beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) for that [deity] are said to consist of twelve measures (mātra);
the water for the feet (pādya), however, should be five measures, and likewise the water for sipping (ācamana).
The water for the guest-offering (arghya) should consist of one measure; the application of fragrant paste, six measures;
the incense should be twelve measures; and the lamp is said to be six measures.
The waving of lights (ārātrika) worship consists of seven [circles], while the collyrium rite (nīrāñjana) consists of sixteen;
thereafter, one should cause the ashes to be distributed, which is said to consist of exactly seven [applications].
The fan should be three *mātrās* in size, the chowrie ten *mātrās*,
the parasol five *mātrās*, and the mirror one *mātrā* of a sage (*munimātra*).
Then one should perform the offering consisting of twenty-four units;
the time for the presentation of the bali-oblation is twenty-five [units] more than that.
The number of breaths in one *nāḍikā* is said to be thirty;
having understood this through the relationship of the worshipper and the worshipped, one should begin the sacrifice.
Śiva alone is the one to be worshipped, and Śakti is said to be the object of worship;
if the worship is deficient, disease shall arise, and if it lacks flowers, there will be loss of wealth.
If the incense is omitted, there is loss of happiness; if the lamp is omitted, there is the destruction of the family;
if the perfume is omitted, leprosy occurs; and if the water is omitted, one becomes miserable.
If the food offering (naivedya) is omitted, there will be famine; if the mantra is omitted, poverty;
if the clothing is omitted, a great disease; and if the fire oblation (homa) is omitted, the loss of strength.
If the bali offering is omitted, there will be the destruction of the village; if the clarified butter is omitted, there is death;
and if the bilva fruits, dūrvā grass, and unbroken rice are omitted, one shall incur fear from enemies.
If the bell is lacking, one becomes deaf; if the mudrā is lacking, there is danger from spirits;
and if the daily fire-ritual is lacking during worship, it shall be fruitless.
If the ceremonial bathing (snapana) and the daily festival (nityotsava) are deficient, there will be fear for the king and the kingdom;
and if they are devoid of grain and wealth, the deity will surely become angry.
From that, the guru becomes destitute of wealth and likewise destitute of mantras;
if the worship is deficient, there is impairment and the destruction of sons, wife, and land.
If the water for the feet and other offerings are lacking, one is humiliated by the Rākṣasas;
therefore, with every effort and preceded by devotion, [one should offer] to the deity.
The maddala drum brings happiness, while the tālakyeśa drum brings liberation; the paṭaha drum removes sin, and the bherī drum increases nourishment.
If one holds a single *praya* in the left hand with equal rhythm (*samatāla*), it brings prosperity;
the *jhallarī* drum fulfills one's desired wishes, and the *kumbha* instrument bestows liberation.
The playing of musical instruments with tuned pipes yields the fruit of ten million sacrifices;
singing on a fine bamboo flute increases one's sons and grandsons.
The joining of beautiful hides, the sound of musical instruments that brings victory,
and the resonance of conch shells— all together destroy every enemy.
Dancing brings about the destruction of disease, and singing increases longevity;
drama results in an increase of grain, and likewise, pure dancing brings auspiciousness.
O Kauṇḍalī, by means of this *āgeṇa*, the king shall attain victory;
it subdues the three worlds, is auspicious, and brings about happiness.
The *kāhala* drum is for the purpose of purifying faults; the *murasā* arises from rain; the *saramaṇḍala* and the lute (*vīṇā*) are associated with heroism and endowed with fortitude.
The *timila* is said to bring victory; the *pāvakatāla* brings the acquisition of wealth.
One who wears [the former] shall attain all perfections (*sarvasiddhi*), while the mark [of the latter] is for subjugating kings.
O Śiva’s twice-born one, having entered the inner sanctum, one should perform the rites for the three eyes, for enjoyment and liberation, and for the subjugation of women with the *katraka* [mantra].
The Brahmins were situated in the inner pavilion for the purpose of recitation,
while the initiated ascetics were situated in the outer pavilion.
For the women of royal families, it is situated in the dance pavilion;
for uninitiated women who are the wives of others, it is situated at the gateway of the city gate.
One should perform the ritual after seeing flowers of all various species; this is declared to be the entry into the temple. Now hear the procedure for the flowers.
The guardian of the eastern gate, Nandīkāla, has been installed;
and the guardians of the southern gate, Daṇḍī and Muṇḍī, have been installed.
And the two gatekeepers of the western door are Bṛṅgīśa and Vijaya in sequence;
the two gatekeepers of the northern door are Ananta and Pāśupati.
The dark-colored Nandī is established on the south,
while the two Mahākālas, resembling saffron in hue, are established on the north.
A staff-bearer resembling Indra should be stationed on his right side;
however, one with a shaven head and white form should be placed on the left side.
One should place Bhṛṅgī and Mayūragrīva, resembling [the colors] of a bee and a peacock's neck respectively, on the right in order;
and on the left, one should place Vijaya, who is joined with one having the luster of coral.
One should place Ananta, who has a dense form, on the right side;
and the wise one should place Paśupati, who is blue in color, on the left side.
Nandīśa should have a staff in his hand; Kāla should be holding an axe;
Daṇḍīśa should have a sword in his hand; and Muṇḍīśa should be joined with a skull-bowl.
Bhṛṅgī, however, should hold a spear in his hand; Vijaya is the bearer of a trident;
Ananta should have a thunderbolt in his hand; and Paśupati likewise holds a noose.
All [the deities] should be made three-eyed and four-armed, or alternatively, two-armed;
they should be endowed with all ornaments and adorned with crowns and other finery.
The waist-belt, however, is joined with Ścapūra and Ścannavīra;
endowed with these characteristics, it is installed at every door.
At the gate of the inner circle (antarmaṇḍalaka), Nandi and Kāla are installed;
likewise Bhuvaṅga, Pataṅga, Jalika, and the others are the presiding deities (adhidevatās).
One should worship Vimala and Subāhu on the two door-panels;
having worshipped the lintel and the threshold, one should worship the ring of the Sun and Moon.
In the cavity is the ninefold power; by means of the weapon-mantra, one should proceed to the base.
Likewise, there are Gaṇeśa, Bhāratī, Lakṣmī, Nandin, and Gaṅgā.
Mahākāla, Yamunā, and the weapons are proclaimed as the Vāstus;
one should first worship the Bull with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, in due order.
In the inner enclosure (antarhāra), however, Bhṛṅgin and Īśa are to be installed in sequence, starting from the center;
likewise, Ananta and Paśupati should be placed in the ritual arrangement.
Kumbhodara and Mahodara, endowed with great gate-towers, were at the two ends; they possessed great strength, held staffs in their hands, and acted for the benefit of the bhūtas.
Having thus described the ritual for the worship of the doors, now hear the procedure for the worship of the retinue:
[one should worship] the bull, white in color, with sharp horns and great strength.
The four-footed form is the Veda, while the horn is the form of Agni;
Āditya is the cowherd, and likewise Rudra is the mouth.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra [worship] the Bull, who consists of all the gods,
as he arises from the earth in five colors at the time of the creation of the universe.
Situated in the midst of the seven oceans, it is the entrance into the world of mortals;
it consists of four quarters and the four Vedas, and is thus the very form of Dharma.
Bhīṣaṇa is said to be at the tip of the hair; Vāsuki spoke from the ears;
Mahendra is in the nose, and the Moon and Sun are in the eyes.
The tooth is to be known as belonging to Rudra, while the tongue is indeed Vaiṣṇava;
the lower lip has Brahmā as its deity, and the right horn belongs to Skanda.
Vighneśa is on the left horn, Sadāśiva on the forehead,
Śiva is said to be in the middle of the horns, and Sarvatīrthaka at the tip of the tail.
Thus, at the time of sacrifice, the wise one should meditate [on the deity] as wearing red garments, formidable, with hair standing erect and a topknot.
