One should visualize the Fire-god mounted upon a goat, joined with spears and iron clubs, adorned with garlands of flames, and surrounded by his seven tongues.
Resembling cow’s milk in its whiteness, with two arms and two eyes,
he is endowed with a circle of rays and wears a crown of lapis lazuli.
One should represent the Moon together with Rohiṇī, holding a white water-lily (kumuda) in his hand.
I shall now describe the characteristics of the Mothers according to their colors, vehicles, and emblems.
One should fashion a beautiful image seated in the lotus posture; this is called the "Lakṣaṇa" [type]. It has four arms and large eyes, resembling molten gold.
Her hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; she holds a water-pot and a rosary;
she has a swan as her emblem, is mounted upon a swan, and wears a crown of matted locks.
Seated upon a red lotus throne is Brahmāṇī, whose form is that of Brahmā;
she possesses the luster of a conch, a kunda flower, and the moon, and is dark-complexioned, holding an axe.
She has three eyes, the luster of white color, holds a trident in her hand, and has the bull as her emblem;
she grants boons and fearlessness, and her hands are joined with a rosary of beads.
O Śambhu, she who wears a crown of matted locks is the ornament of Maheśvarī;
she is joined with the cock-bannered one and adorned with breasts like saffron.
She is joined with a spear and a club, her hands granting boons and fearlessness;
she is firmly mounted upon [a vehicle] and rests upon the fruit of the udumbara tree.
One should have the goddess, the foremost of the planets, fashioned wearing silken garments,
holding a conch and a discus, with her hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
She was adorned with a crown and diadem, decorated with necklaces and armlets;
she possessed beautiful breasts and a lovely face, was dark-complexioned, and in the full bloom of youth.
One should have the goddess Vaiṣṇavī fashioned, seated upon a rājavṛkṣa tree and joined with the one whose banner is Garuḍa; thereafter, listen to [the description of] Vārāhī.
She possesses a great form of blue color, radiant with a crown of caskets;
she wears black garments, has fangs, and a face like that of a boar standing upon a boar.
The goddess, who has four arms and a beautiful face, is seated beneath a banyan tree;
she possesses four faces, and her hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
The wise one should cause her to be adorned with golden horns and joined with sandalwood trees;
and he should likewise join her hand, which displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, with a *karañja* tree.
Adorned with the lion-banner and embellished with all ornaments,
it was joined with the elephant-banner and equipped with parasols and chowries.
She has the color of a red mandala, is radiant with a crown and tiara,
is joined with a vajra-noose, and is accompanied by a wish-fulfilling tree.
One should have the goddess Indrāṇī fashioned, adorned with divine flowers;
the wise one should have Cāmuṇḍī fashioned, possessing a luster like a dark rain cloud.
She holds a trident joined with a skull, is dark-complexioned, and has four arms;
her hair stands erect, she is adorned with conch shells and bells, and her limbs are bound by serpents.
She is joined with a banner of the hungry ghosts (pretadhvaja) and rests upon a banyan tree;
she is dark-complexioned yet red in hue, with arms blazing like fire. With her two hands she holds the eight divine weapons:
a trident and a vetāla in her right hands, and in her left hands a sword, a hand-drum (ḍamaruka), and a skull-cup.

O you who hold a bell aloft and a shield, accompanied by the plow-bearer, possessing a fierce aspect and three eyes—this is the form of Cāmuṇḍā; O Bhadrakālī, who brings the worlds under your control, salutations to you!
One should fashion Vighneśa as before, endowed with all the characteristic marks:
saffron-colored, four-armed, with the face of an elephant, wearing a crown and a *guṇḍa* ornament.
Holding a goad, a sweetmeat, and a noose in his teeth, possessing the form of Gaṇanātha with eyes like fire,
resembling the rising sun, he is eternally in the form of a child.
Four-armed and three-eyed, adorned with all ornaments,
endowed with necklaces and armlets, and likewise having a peacock as his vehicle.
In his right hands, however, he holds the Abhaya-vajra and the Varada-aṅkuśa;
in his left, he is coral-colored, possesses twenty arms and six faces,
and holds the Śakti, arrow, sword, Abhaya, banner, and mace.
With a bow and vajra in his left hand and a fierce expression, he holds a trident and a lotus, possessing the form of the six-faced one.
His face, possessing the luster of the moon, is crimson like vermilion; his body is adorned with divine ornaments such as armlets and necklaces, bestowing the bliss of heaven.
Holding a lotus, the gesture of fearlessness, a spear, and a cock, he is smeared with red unguents and clad in a silken garment.
We worship Subrahmaṇya; let those who bow down with fear be liberated from their terror.

This is Skanda Kumāra, seated upon a lotus, possessing the color of saffron, endowed with four arms; his right hands hold a spear and grant the gesture of fearlessness, while his left hands hold a thunderbolt and a javelin.
The characteristics of the youth have been described; now hear of the form of Lakṣmī.
In the center of that [lotus], she is seated comfortably upon a lotus, having performed her ablution with water from two jars held by two elephants.
In her right [hands], she holds a boon-granting gesture along with a lotus, and the great Lakṣmī; in her left [hands], she holds a bilva fruit and a lotus, and is of a beautiful yellow hue.
The characteristics of Lakṣmī have been declared; now the characteristics of Jyeṣṭhā are being stated:
she who is joined with daughters and sons, and endowed with the "crow-banner" (kākadhvaja).
One should have the goddess fashioned wearing red garments, adorned with pearl ornaments,
endowed with all types of jewelry, and possessing a beautiful complexion.
The characteristics of Jyeṣṭhā have been declared; now the characteristics of Durgā are being described:
she is clothed, has dark hair, and possesses the form of a blue lotus petal.
She has a beautiful face, is adorned with all ornaments,
possesses four arms, and holds a discus, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons.
Adorned with a girdle of *kuśa* grass, she rests upon the head of a buffalo;
she carries a pair of red lotuses in her two hands, is exceedingly beautiful,
and wears a successful coral and golden bodice as her auspicious second garment.
Wearing jeweled earrings, necklaces, armlets, ear-ornaments, and flower-caskets,
you are the sun consisting of eternal awakening, the Lord whose hand is the architect of the universe.
Possessing a divine form that protects the world, resembling a lotus bud,
endowed with a halo of light, with a neck like a conch shell and beautiful eyes.
Adorned with a crown and a casket, joined by the dawn and the early morning,
the great Lord holds a lotus grasped in both hands.
One should fashion [the image] endowed with all the primary marks as having the form of the Sun; thus the characteristics of the Sun have been declared. Now hear the procedure for the Kṣetrapāla.
In the northeastern quarter of the field, one should worship according to the prescribed rite;
the trident, skull-bowl, axe, and noose are recorded as his weapons.
It is declared to be threefold according to the division of the three qualities:
the sāttvika is white in form, while the rājasa is red in color.
The Tāmasa [form] is black in color and is declared to be of three kinds;
the Tāmasa is said to have eight arms, while the Rājasa should have six arms.
He has four arms specifically according to the Sāttvika rite;
his weapons are remembered as the trident, the skull-bowl, the chisel, and the noose.
With hair standing erect and beautiful round eyes,
he has a body with curled locks and is adorned with serpent ornaments.
Naked in form, yet possessing three eyes and adorned with anklets on his feet,
the glorious one stands upon a dog, graced with eight arms.
In the right hands, he holds a trident, a noose, a sword, and a khaṭvāṅga;
in the left hands, he holds a skull-cup, an axe, a shield, and a bell.
He may be surrounded by vetālas, hosts of bhūtas, and dogs;
one endowed with these characteristics is known as Kṣetrapāla.
Nirvāṇa, non-conceptual, incomparable, all-pervading, changeless, protector, the syllable *huṃ*, with fangs in his mouth, fire-eyed, fierce, in a state of madness;
the syllable *phaṭ*, the destroyer of bonds, with a face marked by a furrowed brow, the Terrifying One, trident-handed.
I bow to Kṣetrapāla, who holds a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), a human skull, and a hand-drum (ḍamaruka).
Wearing a mass of matted hair with red flames, bearing the moon, his body red and composed of radiant energy,
holding in his hands a staff and a skull-bowl, the protector of the world,
the Nirvāṇa who has a dog as his vehicle, the three-eyed one, the tumultuous roar of bliss.
I bow to Vaṭuka, the lord of the bhūtas and piśācas, the auspicious protector of the sacred field (kṣetrapāla).
Then, on the seat in front, she should be worshipped especially:
she who has five heads, even faces, a nose, ten eyes, ten ears, ten arms, ten tridents, and ten supports.
In the throat, heart, and navel as well, there is a sacrificial pedestal (*balipīṭha*) consisting of two feet, which is exceedingly red in color and is the consumer of the offering (*balibhuk*).
Āmoda, Pramoda, the principal Durmukha,
Avighna, and Vighnakartṛ— these are the presiding deities of the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha).
Having drawn a lotus in the east, south, west, north, and in the center, one should worship it in the northeast.
Those of dark-green color [attain] Āmoda; those of black color, Pramoda;
the one with a single face has the luster of crystal, and the two-faced one has the radiance of saffron.
May there be no obstacle for him who has the luster of coral; may he bear the name of the destroyer of obstacles, [overcoming] the yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, bhūtas, gandharvas, and kinnaras.
From the Pitṛs, Dānavas, and Nāgas, up to Brahmā and ending with Īśāna;
beginning with the Praṇava (Oṃ), followed by the word for one's own name in the dative case (caturthī-vibhakti) placed in the middle.
One should append "to all" (*sarvebhyaḥ*) to the specification of the offering ending with *svāhā*.
A brick pedestal, an earthen pedestal, and what appears from the pedestal are said to be the *ābhāsa* (manifestation).
From a reflection it may be like a mural on a wall, or made of wood, or of clay;
among these, that made of wood or clay is superior, and likewise, that made of metal is superior to one made of clay.
Among metals, that which is stone-born is superior; likewise, among stones, that which is jewel-born is best.
One should have the primary image (mūlabera) fashioned from metal or jewels, avoiding stone due to its instability.
It should be performed with the most excellent materials; one should not cause it to be done otherwise.
With *sadyojāta*, however, the lotus root together with its stalk is used for *vāmadeva*.
The Aghora petal is crowded with petals, the Puruṣa has secret filaments, and the Īśāna extends to the tip of the pericarp; thus the lotus is composed of Śiva.
The lotus situated within the womb of power has a blazing liṅga at its center;
the lotus-stalk is the Śiva-liṅga, the Great Lord who pervades all.
I shall describe this Yomipīṭha, which accomplishes all desires and aims:
Vāmāśakti is in the southeast, and Jyeṣṭhāśakti is in the southwest.
Raudrī is in the direction of the wind (the northwest), Ambikā in the northeast,
Śubhākṣī in her own desired eastern direction, and likewise [Śivā] in the south.
One should worship the Bhagas of dark complexion in the western part of the Bhaga and in the northern Bhagadarpiṇī, using their respective initial names.
The power of the directions (Dikśakti) is white in color, while the power of the directions is red in color;
she has three eyes and four arms, with her hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and protection.
Endowed with these characteristics, one should become oriented toward the Pradhāna.
One should fashion a square pedestal with colors arranged in the form of a *vidyā*;
above that, one should place a sixteen-petaled lotus of even circular shape.
One should worship its petals in sixteen [divisions]; in the middle of each petal, one should worship the seed-syllable resembling the color of milk, adorned with the Bindu and Nāda.
This lotus-vigya is to be known as the vessel of clarified butter; above that, however, is the triple mandala:
namely, the fire-mandala, the sun-mandala, and the moon-mandala.
The base is the triangle of fire, while the remainder is indeed circular;
it should be fashioned in this sequence and worshipped with its respective seed-syllables.
In the center of the triangular maṇḍala, the triple-liṅga is situated in the presence of the gods;
one should then worship it with red [substances] in the middle of that triple-liṅga.
One should worship Romā on the upper part of the vulva,
and at the tip of the three-fold linga, that which possesses a luster equal to the color of gold.
Above that, let there be Vāk, arising like the rising sun,
joined with Bindu and Nāda— the subtle Śakti, the supreme Śiva.
This seed-syllable consists of Śiva and Śakti, and likewise of Umā and Rudra;
it is creation, the lunar day, and dissolution—the entire world of moving and unmoving beings.
Three-eyed and four-armed, engaged in the consecration of joyful play,
resembling pure crystal, with beautiful breasts and in the full bloom of youth.
Adorned with pearl ornaments, beautifully radiant in white garments,
equipped with a bow, and captivating with her jeweled crown.
In the right [hand] one should cause her to hold the yoni-mudrā and a rosary for recitation above it;
in the left, the wise one should know that she holds the amṛta-hand and a book.
One should worship this Goddess, whose form is Śakti, and Śiva, who is gross, subtle, and supreme,
by means of the path of the five enclosures (pañcāvaraṇa) with fresh flowers.
The wise man, having turned facing north, should pay homage to the sandals of the venerable former teachers and meditate upon them all.
O Mahādeva, the Liṅga situated embraced by Umā is called Nāha;
it is all-pervading and rises above the seven cosmic eggs.
A wise person should worship the infinite one known as the Śivaliṅga;
it is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
One should worship each [deity] with its respective state and with its respective mantra;
one should worship that which resides within the liṅga, for invocation and dismissal are supreme.

Having placed his hands joined in *añjali* at his heart with flowers, the practitioner, having attained a state of equanimity (*samarasībhāva*) through devotion toward the great *prāsāda-mantra* which has as its sphere the partless (*aniṣkala*),
should meditate upon the power of the *vaṃ-krama* within the *nāda* and likewise within the *bindu*.
The invocation of the deity should take place in the abode of Śakti at the conclusion of the sequential ritual.
Just as the embryo resides within the egg, so Śiva resides within the *liṅga*;
the individual soul (*jīva*), supported by the side of the Mother, is full and possesses the nature of the Self.
Through devotion, mantra, ritual action, and yoga, the partless Śiva becomes present;
having formed a handful of flowers and being permeated by the sentiment of Śiva, one should remain focused on Him.
One should ascend by the sequence of three measures and so forth until reaching the river and other such points;
just as fire, though present in wood, blazes forth when churned, O Guha.
And so, through the application of devotion, dispassion, and the offering of mantra with joined palms,
there is a manifestation [of the inner fire], just as the fire situated at the tip of a blade of grass is revealed within the wood.
In the same way, when one [teacher] speaks through consciousness, it is not contradicted by the practitioner;
just as fire contained within a vessel may be made to blaze by means of the wind.
And thus, by means of the linga alone, the Lord Śiva is born;
he undergoes dissolution within it, for he abides in the midst of the linga.
Just as fire, though inferior, remains pervading a piece of wood and becomes stained by it,
so too that which resides in one part of the wood becomes stained through its application.
The practitioner who possesses the mantra is like a lamp with wood; he who possesses the cloth is like a lamp with oil.
By meditating and meditating again, it should be known that the all-pervading Lord exists like fire.
That which is the bringing down of the deity from the excellent palace is called invocation (āvāhana);
the turning [of the deity] away from that is then called dismissal (udvāsana).
There is no invocation (āvāhana) nor dismissal (udvāsana), especially because there is the mark of the learned (śiṣṭa). Śiva, Sadāśiva, and Maheśa are indeed the three forms.
Devoid of the signified and the signifier, beyond the reach of speech and mind,
endowed with all qualities of omniscience, the Lord is the abode of all reality.
Thus has Śiva in his manifested state been described; now those who are partless (niṣkala) shall be proclaimed as bestowing fame.
The manifest (sakala) is endowed with the partless and consists of thirty-eight constituent parts (kalās).
The path of the parts (kalādhvan) is complete with its stated limbs; it possesses the hair of the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan);
it is endowed with the skin of the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan); and it is joined with the blood of the path of mantras (mantrādhvan).
The six paths beginning with the word (*pada*) consist of the channels (*sirā*), flesh, marrow, and semen; this is the sixfold path of Sadāśiva, and its vital breath is known as Śiva.
Complete with the heart and other limbs, he assumes a manifest form during meditation;
however, in the state of the partless reality, he is therefore both manifest and partless (sakalaniṣkala).
I shall now describe in detail the form of Sadāśiva:
it has the luster of jasmine, the moon, and crystal, and is adorned with a crown of matted locks.
They possess five faces, and each face has three eyes;
they are adorned with all ornaments and endowed with ten arms.

In the right hands, he holds a trident, an axe, a sword, a vajra, and the gesture of fearlessness; in the left hands, he holds a noose, a serpent, a bell, and fire, while displaying the boon-granting gesture.
The god was clad in celestial garments, adorned with divine flowers, his limbs anointed with divine perfumes; he possessed a tranquil form and a smiling countenance.
At the time of worship, the wise one should meditate upon the Liṅga in the center:
it resembles the moon, has five faces, is endowed with ten hands, and holds a trident, a ṭaṅka, a sword, a vajra, and displays the gesture of fearlessness.
Holding a noose, the gesture of granting boons, a goad, and a jewel in his left hands,
he is seated upon a white lotus in the form of Sadāśiva.
On the pedestal, one should likewise visualize the goddess Manonmanī, possessing a divine form,
holding a noose and a goad, radiant as a pearl, and in the full bloom of youth.

She was in the full bloom of youth, beautifully dressed, with shapely breasts and a slender waist; her neck was like a conch shell, her limbs were well-proportioned, and she was endowed with fresh vitality.
The goddess’s head is in the south and her excellent feet in the north;
it has a cow-faced [mouth] at the end, joined with arms reaching to the water’s edge,
with the liṅga situated and established within the middle of the womb.
Having established Sadāśiva within the state beyond mind (manonmanī), one attains the very nature of Sadāśiva.
The goddess Vāmā resembles the color of a blue lotus and holds a conch, a discus, and a mace; Jyeṣṭhā shall be yellow in complexion, holding a lotus and a sword, and having lotus-like eyes.
The goddess Raudrī, resembling Raudra, three-eyed and bearing a trident;
and the goddess resembling gold, bearing Kālī and Mudgala.
Kalvikarṇī is smoke-colored, holds a noose in her hand, and is in the full bloom of youth;
Śvetābalavikaraṇī is of great strength and holds a sword in her hand.
The goddess Balapramathanī, who holds a palāśa staff,
is the subduer of all beings and possesses a red-colored skull-cup.
One should place [the deities] from Indra up to Īśāna in the enclosure of the pedestal (piṇḍikāvaraṇa);
one should worship each with their respective name-mantra using perfumes and flowers.
One should place the Ātma-tattva on the right, the Vidyā-tattva on the left,
and specifically worship the Śiva-tattva in the center.
The wise one should place the Śiva-tattva, presided over by Rudra, into the wine;
he should do so while performing sacrifice to the liṅgas or while stationed within the image (kautuka).
Even when seated before a *liṅga* or the like, or upon a mandala or sacrificial ground, one approaches [the deity] by means of the mantra; this is known as the invocation (*āvāhana*) through prayer.
Having established [the deity] upon the seat, one should likewise perform the installation of the measure (mitīcasthāpana),
the welcome accompanied by mantra, and the rite for making [the deity] well-disposed (sumukhīkaraṇa).
The thread should be at the side of the arms, and the junction of the threads should be at the back;
then, the knower of mantras should invoke the deity with the Sadyojāta mantra.
One should establish [the deity] with Vāmadeva and bring it into proximity with Aghora;
one should perform the rite of restraint with Puruṣa and worship with Īśāna.
The western face is Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva is likewise on the other [the north];
the southern face is Aghora, while the eastern face is Tatpuruṣa.
Īśāna is indeed remembered as the upward-facing face; thus he is known as the five-faced one.
Īśāna has an upward face with the luster of crystal; to the east is Tatpuruṣa, with the splendor of saffron; and to the south is the face of Aghora, resembling collyrium.
The eastern face is like a thunderbolt or similar to sin; likewise, the northern is the face of the newborn, while this western one has a luster equal to cow's milk.
Brahmā is indeed the face of Sadyojāta, Janārdana is Vāmadeva, Aghora has Rudra as its presiding deity, and Tatpuruṣa is likewise Īśvara.
Īśāna and Sadāśiva are proclaimed as the presiding deities;
the supreme [state] whose essence is Sadāśiva should be known as Manonmanī.
One should offer water for the feet (pādya) once for each foot, beginning with the right foot;
one should offer water for sipping (ācamana) into the mouths with an uninterrupted stream of water.
Thereafter, one should offer the head-arghya with perfumes and flowers as is appropriate,
and perform the consecration upon the head with pure water and other substances.
Standing either in the southeast or in the southwest, one should worship the deity;
an ablution should be performed, bathing [the deity] upon the heads of Śiva.
To Śiva who has arrived here, one should offer water for the feet (pādya) at his feet with the heart-mantra;
one should give water for sipping (ācamana) into his mouths, and one should cause the respectful offering (arghya) to be given upon his head.
One should perform the placement of the thirty-eight *kalās*, beginning with the crown (*makuṭa*) and following the sequence,
while reciting the five Brahmans, the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), and the *vyomavyāpin* mantra.
Thereafter, one should bathe [the deity] with water, and also with curd, milk, and ghee;
likewise with coconut water, honey, and the five products of the cow (brahmapañcaka).

One should perform the consecration with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and the Brahmakūrca mixture; then, with the Hṛdaya mantra, one should apply rice-flour paste to the top of the liṅga.
Having first treated it with auspicious water, one should rub it with sour gruel;
thereafter, one should smear it with turmeric and bathe it with scented water.
Afterwards, the wise practitioner should offer water for sipping (ācamana) at the five faces;
having performed the smearing with cloth, he should especially do so for the liṅga and the pedestal.
One should cause a flower to be placed upon the heads with the *hṛdaya* mantra;
one should strike the bell there and remove the curtain.
One should cause the garment, the sacred thread, the perfume, the crown, the earrings,
as well as the necklace, the armlets, and the garland to be offered with the heart-mantra.
Having offered incense and a lamp with the heart-mantra, thereafter [offer] water and collyrium to the mouth,
the two eyes, the two nostrils, the two ears, the chest, and the two feet.
Each [lamp] has the form of the *praṇava* (Om); these are the characteristics of the lamps.
I shall now describe the rite for self-protection, which brings happiness to all living beings.
At the end of the evening, for the sake of the world's eyes and for the purpose of cessation,
one should perform the protection of the night, concluding with incense and lamps.
Having performed the consecration slowly, the preceptor should take up a flower;
[he should also prepare] an ointment of ground āmalaka and other ingredients, as well as cow-products such as clay, water, milk, curd, and clarified butter.
By bathing with honey, sugarcane juice, coconut water, and fragrant water, one obtains a conch-shell mark.
Having stirred the cloth together with scents and flowers, one should prepare the food offering,
incense, and lamp using the *śāstrapuṣpa* in the ritual.
If it is devoid of protection from the rays [of the sun], there will be destruction for the children;
therefore, one should draw a square mandala either in front of the linga or in front of the image.
Having prepared five vessels for the support of the apertures, the support of the arrows, and likewise the single support, one should take them up and place them at the heart.
One should sprinkle [the offering] with the *puruṣa* mantra itself and display the *dhenu-mudrā*.
One should perform the worship of the lamp, however, not with flour made of *śāli* rice.
The width is four finger-breadths and the height is two finger-breadths;
the middle of the lip is said to be one finger-breadth, having the shape of the full moon.
One should place a lamp in the center of that, and lamps in the four directions as well;
one should arrange five lamps provided with cow's ghee.
Among the vessels for the Varkīs, one should place a neem vessel and mustard seeds,
and one should add cotton seeds and salt into four vessels.
Having worshipped the lamp-stand, the most excellent preceptor should perform [the rite]:
having rotated three times with cotton seeds, salt, dūrvā grass, sesame, unbroken rice, mustard, and nimba leaves, he should cast [these] along with ashes and lamp-vessels upon the head of Śiva.
One should worship with the heart-mantra itself and display the trident-mudrā;
having worshipped the fire according to the rules, the wise one [should perform the rite] with the *agni-ja* mantra.
Amidst the sounding of conchs and kettledrums, and with hymns and auspicious musical instruments,
one should first offer water for the feet (*pādya*) using the *astra-mantra*, and then offer water for sipping (*ācamana*) using the *netra-mantra*.
The wise one, having whirled it three times with the lamp itself using the *śikhā-mantra*, [should proceed].
Then, having performed the whirling at the head and likewise the whirling of the feet,
the wise practitioner should whirl the three [limbs] from the knees up to the top of the head.
Having applied the divine [mantras] in downward order, revolving them around the liṅga,
one should cause the ashes of Śambhu to be bestowed, as well as the binding of the directions with the Astra-mantra.
With the tip of the ring finger, one should cause protection to be bestowed by means of ashes;
whether by a devotee of Rudra, by those who fear the Gaṇas, or by a Brahmin, the vessels [should be prepared].
One should place the fire, equipped with all musical instruments, either at the front of the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) or elsewhere; moreover, one should especially cause a lamp to be lit.
The wise one should burn mustard seeds, salt, cotton, and white mustard there with the fire of a lamp, using the seed-syllable of fire (RAḤ).
One should offer betel-leaf accompanied by all ritual offerings,
and one should delight her with fans and whisks near her face.
Having covered [the head] above with an umbrella, one should show a mirror to the face;
the ten mudrās should be employed as described in the *Darśapāṇis*.
The ten mudrās are proclaimed to extend from Vajrā to Padmā; this is called the "Eye-Salve" (nīrāñjana). Now hear about the fifth enclosure.
The Embryo (garbha), the Vidyā, the Gaṇeśas, the Lokapālas, and the Three Eyes—
this is declared to be the fivefold enclosure (pañcāvaraṇa) which bestows all prosperity.

The first [altar] should be for the limbs of Brahmā; then for the Vidyeśvaras, the Gaṇeśvaras, the Guardians of the Quarters, and the Ten Weapons; and finally for the Lord, according to the sequence of the five enclosures.
Having seen [the deity] within the inner enclosure, one should worship at the base of the lotus;
and in the center of the lotus, the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas), and half as many Gaṇeśas.
Then one should worship the world-protectors on the tips of the lotus petals and the weapons;
one should worship Tatpuruṣa in the east and Aghora in the south.
One should worship Sadyojāta in the west and Vāmadeva in the north;
one should worship Īśāna above the liṅga with perfumes and flowers.
Having worshipped the heart-mantra in the southeast (pāvaka), one should worship the crest-mantra (śikhā) in the southwest (naiṛti);
the armor-mantra (kavaca) in the northwest (vāyu), and the head-mantra (śiras) in the northeast (vaiśāna).
One should worship the weapon (astra) in the south and the eye (nayana) in the northeast;
[the colors] are white, saffron, black, red, and resembling white.
The five Brahmās should have five faces, three eyes, and four arms;
they hold a trident and a skull in their hands, and are endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons.
It is said that Īśāna is peaceful, while others are remembered as fierce (raudra);
[their colors are] white, yellow, reddish, red, dark-blue, and black.
The six limbs, beginning with color, have three eyes and four arms;
they are endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons, and are equipped with the ṭaṅka and the trident.
Red, white, blue, yellow, black, and saffron-colored, resembling the luster of vermilion and añjana— these are, in order, the colors of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas).
One should worship specifically from Indra to Īśāna;
thus is the enclosure of the Vidyeśvaras. Now hear about the enclosure of the Gaṇeśvaras.
And Nandīśa, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgīśa,
Vināyaka, Vṛṣabha, Skanda, the Goddess, and likewise Caṇḍeśvara.
Four-armed and three-eyed, he has the color of a blue lotus;
he bestows fearlessness and boons, and holds a lance and a trident.
The lord Bhṛṅgīśa is four-armed and three-eyed, tawny in hue;
he holds an elephant goad in his right hand and a trident and the gesture of granting boons in his left.
One should meditate upon the elephant-faced one, who has three eyes, the luster of saffron, and four arms;
he holds a noose and a tusk in his right hands, while in his left hands he holds a goad and a sweetmeat ball.
The Naga wears a sacred thread, while the Lord of the Ganas has hanging lips;
the Bull is white in form, possessing sharp horns and great strength.
Divine in form and exceedingly beautiful, resembling molten gold;
Mahāsena is red in color, possessing three eyes and four arms.

In her right hands she holds the Abhaya-vajra and the Varada-mudrā with a goad; in her left, she has two eyes, two arms, is dark-complexioned, and [the other] Gaurī holds a blue lotus in her right hand.
One should especially worship [the deities] from Indra up to Īśāna;
thus is the Gaṇeśa enclosure. Now hear about the Lokeśa enclosure.
One should worship Indra and the others, ending with Īśāna; having worshipped Brahmā in the northeast, one should likewise worship Viṣṇu in the southwest.
One should worship the Seven Mothers between Gaṇeśa and Pāla; and on the right side, one should likewise worship Vīrabhadra and Vināyaka.
Thus is the fourth enclosure; now hear of the fifth enclosure:
it is said to consist of the weapons of the world-protectors, beginning with the vajra and ending with the lotus.
The ten weapons are the vajra, the śakti, the staff, the sword, the noose, as well as the goad, the mace, the trident, the discus, and the lotus.
Yellow like lightning, fruit-like, and dark blue; situated like a dark cloud;
ruby-colored, frost-white, variegated, and reddish-white.
In that [mandala], the Śakti is female, the Pāśa is neuter, and the Cakra is male;
the remainder is in the form of a man, with one face and two hands.
The armor of weapons has been described; one should worship them below the tips of the petals, worshipping each with its own name-mantra using perfumes and flowers.
One should worship specifically from Indra up to Īśāna;
this is declared to be the five-fold enclosure (pañcāvaraṇa), along with the food offering and side dishes.
"O God, destroyer of Tripura, tell me how one should offer the mantra-food that is combined with pieces of sugar-cane, mixed with clarified butter, and immersed in curd."
The mantra is said to be the secret; that which ends with *mad* is called food (*anna*). That which is the secret rice (*odana*) is described as the food of the mantra.
Having distributed three-quarters [of the offering] onto the pedestal and other vessels,
one should properly arrange the sacrificial oblation (havis) consisting of that which is to be drunk, licked, and sucked.
Having sprinkled [the offering] with the heart-mantra and purified it by means of the piercing [mantra],
one should transform it into nectar with the "cow’s milk" mantra and place the flower upon the food offering.
One should offer the food offering (naivedya) with the right hand, as well as the excellent drinking water;
the food offering is presented at the five faces, and likewise again at the upper face.
The milk and water mixed together are the milk-rice drink of the swans;
the offering of food for the gods, when accompanied by the mantra, brings satisfaction equal to that.
Just as the core of the wood-apple fruit is [consumed] even when eaten by an elephant,
so too should one offer it for the enjoyment of the deity using the mantra alone.
Having offered water for sipping from the heart-mantra and performed the binding of the directions, the Guru, having again offered water for sipping, should present it to Caṇḍeśa.
Thereafter, the wise practitioner should cause betel-leaf to be offered, especially with the Sadyojāta mantra;
he should present the offering to the retinue and maintain the perpetual sacred fire.
For the sake of the welfare of the world of mortals,
one should especially worship the ninefold forms of the Lord with constant devotion and perfect concentration.
The wise man should offer the protective oblation and maintain the perpetual sacred fire.
For the sake of the welfare of the mortal world,
one should especially worship the nine forms of the Lord with constant devotion and perfect concentration.
The three lesser [rites] end with the lamp, the offering, and the bali;
the three middling [rites] end with the fire-oblation, the festival, and the hymn of praise.
The *saukhyānta*, the *culukodānta*, and the *prāṇāgnihotra* are declared to be the triad of the highest [mantras], which bestow the fruit of their worship along with the *sāpūja*.
Worship ending with the lamp is declared [the lowest]; worship ending with the food offering (nivedya) is the middle;
worship ending with the bali offering is declared to be the pacificatory (śāntika); indeed, these three constitute the inferior triad of fruits.
That which ends with the *homa* is declared to be *vijaya*; that which ends with the festival (*utsava*) is the *śāntika*;
that which ends with hymns of praise (*stotra*) is declared to be the *pauṣṭika*. Indeed, the fruit of these three middle ones is middling.
It brings an end to suffering, increases liberation, bestows prosperity even when taken in a mere mouthful, and makes the *prāṇāgnihotra* fruitful; such is its ninefold fruit.
One should worship the deity along with the limbs, secondary limbs, and minor limbs; this is remembered as being threefold:
the water for bathing, the water for the feet, and likewise the water for sipping.
Clothing, ornaments, fragrant substances, and ointments,
as well as the water-offering (arghya) and the mantra-flower, are proclaimed to constitute the ritual with all its constituent parts.
The secondary offerings (upāṅga) should consist of incense and lamps, as well as the protection against the setting sun and ashes;
likewise, the parasol, the fly-whisk, the mirror, and the vision [of the deity].
Accompanied by dance and song, it is proclaimed as the "Upāṅga";
having performed the offering of food, the presentation of oblations, and the fire sacrifice, one should carry out the rite.

The "eternal festival" (nityotsava) is proclaimed as being performed for every limb, beginning with the water-offering (culuka). There are ten services (upacāras), and including the offerings from the lamp up to the sacrificial oblation (havis), there are sixteen.
The *bali* offerings consist of twenty-five and thirty-six [items], ending with the *dāṇḍa*;
likewise, there is the invocation (*āvāhana*), the water for honor (*arghya*), the water for the feet (*pādya*), and the water for sipping (*ācamanīyaka*).
Bathing, clothing, the sacred thread, incense, the lamp, and dismissal—these ten services (upacāras) are to be known; the worship of Śiva concludes with the lamp.
Invocation and installation, water for the feet, water for sipping, and the respectful offering;
bathing, clothing, the sacred thread, and ornaments, along with perfumes and flowers.
One should worship at the conclusion of the oblation with the sixteen services (upacāras), including incense, lamps, food offerings, prostration, and the ritual dismissal.

Bathing, garments, and ointments; flowers, incense, lamps, and oblations; betel-leaf with mouth-perfume and water for the feet; great music and dance; fire-offerings accompanied by the primary offerings to the spirits; and daily festivals together with hymns of praise.
This is the complete worship of Śambhu accompanied by the sixteen ancillary offerings.
Having performed the invocation and offered a welcome accompanied by salutations,
and having provided water for sipping (ācamana) and the respectful offering (arghya), one should offer a garment and an upper cloth of yellow silk.
Ornaments, incense, flowers, as well as incense sticks and lamps, eye-ointment, and then the mudrās; these are for the worship of the covering of vision.
The offering of food, the rite of fire-oblation, and likewise the presentation of the bali-offering;
the hymn of praise, the recitation, the prostration, and finally, at the conclusion of the festival, the ritual dismissal.
The propitiatory rite (śāntika) is said to consist of twenty-five services (upacāra),
beginning with the seat (āsana), the removal of obstacles (apāsana), the water for honor (arghya), the welcome (svāgata), and the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana).
Water for the feet, water for sipping, water for bathing, a garment, and a sacred thread;
ornaments, fragrance, flowers, incense, a lamp, and likewise the arghya offering.
The ritual of the collyrium-free eyes, the chowrie, the parasol, and the mirror;
the vision of the ten mudrās, and the worship of the five enclosures.
The offering of food, the rite of fire-oblation, the giving of bali, as well as recitation,
meditative concentration, hymns of praise, meditation, music, and instrumental performance;
The dance, the offering of arghya, and its dismissal constitute the thirty-six modes of service;
for the sake of another, O Lord, the worship of the deity at the conclusion of the dance is performed in this manner during the rite of nourishment (pauṣṭika).

In the middle of the three [sessions], at the conclusion of the festival, the wise one should perform the twenty-five-fold ritual service; during the half-watch of the night, he should worship and honor with the eight-limbed offering.

One should perform worship especially with water for the feet, water for sipping, the arghya offering, fragrance, flowers, and incense, even without the fire-oblation, the food-offering, or the festival.
Having offered a lamp and an oblation at the half-watch [of the night],
the daily worship of the gods, situated within the enclosure wall in their celestial chariots, is performed with the eight limbs.
One should go to that root-abode of the gods, where there is a perpetual festival. Worship of Śiva in the morning brings welfare to the twice-born and is dear to Brahmā; it is nourishing (pauṣṭika).
Worship of Śiva at midday brings welfare to kings and is dear to Viṣṇu; it is pacifying (śāntika).

The worship of Śiva in the evening is beneficial for Vaiśyas and dear to Śambhu; it bestows happiness and is beneficial for Śūdras. At midnight, O Umā, it leads to the pleasure of Bhava and fulfills the desires of those who seek them.
Seven times for each of the three [offerings]: perfumes, water for the hands (arghya), incense, lamps, and eight flowers;
thereafter, four coverings, and finally, the striking of the bell.
In the acts of invocation, the offering of water (arghya), the washing of the feet (pādya), as well as bathing, sipping water (ācamana),
the presentation of food (naivedya), and the ritual dismissal (visarjana), one should employ water seven times.
One should employ the three fragrances (the "three scents") during the offering of water, the unguent, and the bath;
likewise, one should properly offer the water of honor (arghya) at the invocation, at the conclusion of the worship, and at the time of dismissal.
One should perform the dismissal at the time of seating and worship, and at the conclusion of the worship;
one should worship during the four periods when [the deity] is covered by a concealed cloth.
One who is afflicted by a foul disease, one who has been cast out, an atheist,
one who defiles the sacred tradition, one who is deficient in limbs, one of wicked conduct, one devoid of initiation, and likewise a lecher.
One who is a *kuṇḍa*, a *golaka*, a heretic (*pāṣaṇḍī*), or a Śaiva;
one who sells the Vedas, or even those who sell sacred texts.
One who steals the property of Śiva shall have a diseased skin and a deformed thumb;
indeed, the thief of Śiva’s property is a traitor to Śiva and a sinner.
One who steals the teacher's property, one who betrays the teacher, a sinner, one of foul speech, one of wicked conduct, a fool, and one who reviles the teacher— [these are the ones to avoid].
If one looks [at the painting] out of negligence, the worship will become fruitless;
likewise, if one carries the cloth-painting during the three times of bathing, incense-offering, and festivals.
At all other times, one should wrap it with a cloth;
or else, in another manner, specifically during the time for painting the cloth.
At the time of worship, one should then offer food offerings and adornments of flowers;
at the time of displaying the mudrās, one should employ gold, jewels, and other such items.
At such times as these, one should begin the rite of the concealed cloth;
indeed, at the time of commencing the worship, at the conclusion of the worship, and when the food offering is presented.
At the beginning and at the end of the daily festival and other rites, one should strike the great bell;
[thereby driving away] the yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, brahmarākṣasas, and bhūtas.
They proceed with the ringing of bells and in the very presence of the deity;
first with instrumental music, then at the end of the steps, and finally upon the gift of garments and the sacred thread.
One should offer water for drinking at the beginning of the offering and dismiss [the deity] at the conclusion;
one should then provide the fivefold sipping of water (ācamana) according to the prescribed rule as is appropriate.
The Vāruṇa, the Saumya, the Āgneya, the Vāyavya, and again the Pārthiva;
then the Vānaspatya is the sixth, while the Prājāpatya is the seventh.
The eighth is the *śivapuṣpa*, which should be employed in the worship of Śiva. The water-born flower is known as belonging to Varuṇa; honey, ghee, and milk belong to Soma.
Incense and lamps belong to the fire element (Āgneya); fans and such belong to the air element (Vāyavya);
bulbs, roots, and so forth belong to the earth element (Pārthiva); and fruits and such belong to the tree element (Vānaspatya).
Then one should worship with food offerings dedicated to Prajāpati, as well as beloved flowers and perfumes;
specifically for each deity, one should perform the worship while striking the bell.
The arka, the lotus, the bilva, the nandyāvarta,
the pāṭalī, the karavīra, the red lotus, and the blue lotus— these constitute the eight.
One should properly apply eight flowers to the two ears, the head, the ear-lobes, the heart, the navel, the private parts, the two knees, and the two feet.
First, a flower should be offered during the ritual ablution with a pure mind;
the offering to the image should be performed with the heart-mantra, and one should worship with that very flower.
By the offering of five flowers, one should worship the five limbs;
likewise, Śiva is worshipped on the eighth—this is declared to be the "Eightfold Flower Offering" (aṣṭapuṣpikā).
Non-violence is the first flower; the flower of forbearance is the second;
the third is the flower of compassion; and the fourth is that which is free from anger.
The fifth is the flower of artificiality, the sixth is the flower of existence;
the seventh is the flower of meditative absorption, while the eighth would be the surpassing one.
The preceptor, through the yoga of mantra and the yoga of ritual action, brings about the presence [of the deity].
At the conclusion of the ritual, having released it from that [state], perform the dismissal.
If one ever performs the rites of incense, lamps, food offerings,
or the worship of *bali* and *liṅga* out of delusion, the *brahmarākṣasas* strike them down.
Having begun with a particular tantra, one should perform worship according to that very tantra;
if one were to worship by means of another tantra, it would swiftly cause the destruction of that [name].
The *jagatphalaka* and the *haviṣya* [offerings] are indeed certain;
therefore, with every effort, one should not perform any other form of worship than these.
It should be performed by a single preceptor located within a single temple;
however, if there should be two or three [preceptors], the king and the kingdom shall be the ones responsible for the performance.
Worship performed at all times without mantras increases the power of the Piśācas and Asuras;
however, it shall always result in the destruction of diseases, thieves, robbers, and the like.
Worship without mantra is declared to be worship at an improper time;
it brings about the destruction of the village, famine, and the ruin of the worshippers.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform worship accompanied by mantra;
and mantra should be known to be of two kinds: Vedic and Tantric.
The southern system is threefold:
mantra according to the rules of mantra, the Vedic, the Tantric, and likewise the Veda-Tantric.
With Vedic mantras, one performs the Vedic rite; likewise with Tantric mantras, the Tantric rite;
and with both Vedic and Tantric mantras, the rite that is both Vedic and Tantric.
The Tantric [path] alone is threefold: Vāma, Yāmala, and Dakṣiṇa;
and the Vaidika is also mixed within both the Vāma and the Yāmala.
One should perform the rites of the Vāmācāra, Yamalatantra, and Dakṣiṇāgama through various mudrās, mantras, and ritual distinctions, using the right hand for the actions of the Dakṣiṇa tradition.
The rites prescribed in the Left-hand Tantras are to be performed with the left hand;
the various types of worship have been fully explained—now hear the procedure for the food offerings.
Then, having purified the ground, one should sprinkle it with water while reciting the heart-mantra;
having strewn [the site] properly with sacrificial grass, one should cover it over with a cloth.
Above that, one should specifically spread a plantain leaf with its tips pointing east and north;
one should then sprinkle it with the *bhūta* [mixture].
Having divided the sacrificial oblation (havis) into three parts, one should offer two portions;
one portion shall remain as the residue in the vessel, along with the side dishes, clarified butter, and soups.
One should accept an abundance of curd and betel leaf,
having placed the weapon-mantra in all directions accompanied by the weapon-mudrā.
The preceptor [should offer] food to be chewed, food to be eaten, drink, food to be sucked, and likewise food to be licked, at the feet of the God of Gods with the heart-mantra.
Having offered flowers with the hands raised, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana);
now hear the procedure for the food offerings (naivedya) and the procedure for the drinking water.
One should fill a clean earthen vessel, resembling molten copper, with water;
the water may be taken from a river, a lake, a well, or other such sources.
It should be filtered through cloth, well-cooled, and seasoned with cardamom and other spices;
one should cause this water, prepared according to this method, to be given while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should offer it to Caṇḍeśa;
the offering of the bali-oblation is proclaimed to be the size of two akṣa-fruits.
One should cause Nandīśa to be offered on the right side of the door,
and one should cause Mahākāla to be offered on the left side of the door.
Then, having given [the offering] to the Bull (Vṛṣabha), one should offer it before the fire in the southeast;
likewise, to the host of Mothers in the south, and again to Nirṛti in the southwest.
To Skanda in the portion of Āyavāruṇa, to Jyeṣṭhā in the region of Vāyu,
to Durgā in the portion of Soma, and to Bhāskara in the north-east.
Then, standing before [the deity], one should especially offer an oblation (bali) upon the pedestal to the yakṣas,
rākṣasas, piśācas, bhūtas, gandharvas, and kinnaras.

The Pitṛs, Dānavas, and Nāgas, from Brahmā to Īśāna and ending with Antaka, [should be addressed] beginning with the Praṇava (Oṃ), followed by their own names in the dative case (caturthī-vibhakti) as the middle term.
One should append "to all" (sarvebhyaḥ) to the specification of the offering ending with "svāhā";
then, having given water for sipping again, accompanied by mouth-perfume.
One should take the powder of cloves, camphor, the powder of small bells (laghudhaṇṭā),
and a full measure of the three fruits, and employ them together.
At the conclusion of the meal, the wise one should offer mouth-perfume dear to Śiva;
O Śambhu, he should cause betel-leaf to be given, along with a *prastha* of fruit for each individual.
The fruit should be four times the amount of the leaf, excluding the stalk and the seed;
it should be combined with horse-powder and accompanied by areca nut.
One should cause that [offering] mixed with sesame oil to be presented to Śiva;
thus is the daily rite described, which the wise man should perform.
One should offer all the sacrificial oblations (nivedyaka) to Caṇḍa and Cāmuṇḍa;
that which has been offered to the Liṅga is known as *nirmālya*. It bestows fame.
One whose self is pure should discard the pure and stainless remains of offerings (nirmālya) upon the ground, in fire, or even in water, as a possession for the sake of the cowherds.
Because the body is bound by impurities, one should not consume leftovers;
however, if one has consumed them through negligence, one should perform the *atikṛcchra* penance.
If one should happen to sneeze there through negligence, a wise person should perform a *prājāpatya* penance;
upon touching [the sneeze], however, one should wash both hands and feet and perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*).
One should sprinkle all the images with pure water using the mantra beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," as well as the floral offerings (nirmālya) and the food offerings (naivedya).
The food of the attendants and others is not to be eaten;
however, the *naivedya* (offering) of Gaṇeśa is said to be edible for everyone.
For those seeking victory, the commander-in-chief, the food offering, and the meal [should be honored];
likewise, for Durgā, the food offered and the meal increase health and well-being.
Food offered to Jyeṣṭhā should be eaten, for it increases one's life;
however, the food offering (naivedya) of Bhāskara is not to be eaten by the devotees of the Sun.
One should offer food and sacrificial oblations (naivedya) for all others as well;
indeed, this offering of food to Mahāmohapuṃs increases one's progeny.
The food offering (naivedya) of the God of Love (Madana) is not to be eaten by Brahmins;
however, the food offering of a Brahmin is indeed fit to be eaten by Brahmins.
The offering to the World-Protectors always bestows health;
the offering to Manmatha is said to be fit for the consumption of all.
Listen now to that which exceeds the Prājāpatya penance as the cause for expiation:
one should perform the Agnihotra for three days in the morning, and then immediately recite the mantra.
For three days, one should recite the *varma-mantra* at sunset while remaining without fire;
then, for five days, one should recite the *pañca-mantra*, and for nine days, one should eat only what is obtained by begging.
For three days one should not eat at all; beyond that, one should especially avoid food.
Then, having meditated upon Sadāśiva, one should thereafter recite the mantra of the face.
One should recite it a thousand times every single day;
this is declared to be the Prājāpatya rite, which cuts away all sins.
One should eat while reciting the *Agnimantra* for the ancestors and mutter the *Guhyaka*.
Hariḥ Om.
One should remain naked for five three-day periods and recite the *Hṛdaya* [mantra] one thousand times.
This is declared to be an extremely difficult penance; if one performs the recitation (japa) every day, the sin committed over seven lifetimes is purified by this alone.
This is declared to be the Prājāpatya rite; now hear the procedure for the perpetual fires (nityāgni).
The most excellent preceptor should establish the fire in the south-eastern quarter according to the prescribed rule.
It should be either square or circular, provided with three girdles;
its width is said to be one *ratna* [of the specific measure], and that same measurement applies to the sacrificial offering (*bali*).
In the west or the south, having prepared a fire-pit with a yoni-shape like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree,
one should establish the fire therein and maintain it without interruption.
One should thoroughly worship the forest fire with offerings up to its very roots;
there, one should worship that which resides in the *liṅga* and that which resides in the fire with oblations of clarified butter.
The preceptor should worship the fire either three times a day or once;
there, the purification, the sweeping, and the smearing with cow dung should be performed in sequence.
One should especially purify [the fire] with the Aghora-weapon mantra;
one should worship the fire with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps.
One should strew the darbha grass and then perform the sprinkling with water;
having offered clarified butter while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should offer the *vyāhṛtis* in their proper sequence.
Having offered with the mantra consisting of the *praṇava*, one should offer sixteen oblations;
having offered the *caru* at the end of that, the *vyāhṛtis* are likewise offered.
Then, having offered the limbs of Brahmā up to the end of the *spṛṣṭa* oblation, one should perform the *hīna* rite;
one should worship the *praṇītā*, the *āghāra*, the fuel-sticks (*samidh*), and the *brahmakūrca*.
Listen now to the ritual for the perpetual fires and the characteristics of the mudrās;
they bring joy to the gods and likewise cause the asuras to melt away.
Because they cause delight and melting, these are proclaimed as mudrās:
the liṅga-mudrā, the namaskāra, the one called tāla, and the śaṅkha-mudrikā.
Surabhimukhī,
vapāhī, niṣura, as well as bījākhyā— the five mudrās— and also dravyamudrā and gipāpyaka.
The mudrā known as Sadāśiva is indeed the Saṃhāra-mudrā;
and the ten mudrās beginning with Vajra belong to Āsanīya Maheśa.
The ṭaṅka seal, the mahāmudrā, the seal called sādākhyā,
the weapon seal, the car seal, and the bow seal— these thirty-two are proclaimed.
O Six-faced One, listen as I shall describe the complete propitiation in brief:
it is threefold, namely the moving, the moving-and-stationary, and the stationary.
It should be known that [the mandala] consists of a movable element made of colored powders, as well as a wall-painting or a cloth-painting;
it may be made of clay adorned with colors, or on a cloth, or as a mural painting.
In those [circumstances], one should worship the deity; bathing brings about all prosperity.
One should display the well-known *liṅga* and *mudrā*, even when [the image] is broken.
Having established [the deity] in the center of the heart, one should offer salutation; this is what is called [the rite]. One should strike with both hands and perform the mudrā to purify it.
At the time of bathing, one should display this conch mudrā;
having done so, it is known as the "remover of sins," and thereafter one should perform the invocation.
That which is known as *sannidha* is especially characterized by total restraint;
it is called the seed-seal (*bījamudrā*), which one should display during the visualization of consciousness.
One should display the five-faced mudrā during the ritual of the faces;
it serves as the material mudrā for them, and one should display it even in the absence of physical materials.
At the time of establishing the one called Śiva, one should display [the mudrās] in the presence of the deity:
the fist-mudrā (muṣṭi), the bound-mudrā (baddha), the dwelling-mudrā (vāsa), the withdrawal-mudrā (hṛta), and the supreme withdrawal-mudrā (sahṛta).
One should perform the mudrā called Āpana and display it at the seat; one should display the Tāla mudrā, known as Mahāśā, at the end of the image.
One should visualize the ten mudrās, beginning with the vajra and ending with the tenth, upon the ten hands;
among these, the *ṭaṅka* mudrā is the great mudrā (*mahāmudrā*), formed by slightly curling [the fingers].
The bow-mudrā (dhanurmudrā) shall bring about the destruction of all enemies;
thus has the sequence of mudrās been fully explained, categorized in pairs.
One should perform the *avakuṇṭhana* (veiling) by means of the *tarpaṇa*, *añjali*, and *mudrās*;
then offer water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), food offerings (*naivedya*), the principal offering (*pradhāna*), and the ritual consecration (*abhiṣecana*).
Garments, ornaments, garlands, and other decorations are offered with both hands;
gifts such as the *darśana* (sight) and others are presented by facing upward, while the *prokṣaṇa* (sprinkling) is performed by looking downward.

A wise person should perform the offering of the *arghya* water with joined palms, the libation (*tarpaṇa*), the invocation (*āvāhana*), and so forth, according to the prescribed rule, using both hands held facing each other.
The sprinkling of the substances for the mantras, even over the surface of the water, is performed with the hand facing downwards; likewise, there is the veiling with the *mṛgāṅka* [mudrā].
Having prepared the bedding and seat, one should arrange for the establishment of the sacred fire;
likewise, the offering of oblations, auspicious moments, and the presentation of perfumes, flowers, and water for honor.
The number of recitations for the consecration, as well as the offering of oblations and so forth, should likewise be performed;
the sprinkling with water from the hand should be done while reciting the Tryambaka mantra.
Joined with exactly three fingers— the middle and the ring fingers—
one should place the substances, deities, and mantras, and cause the offering of scents and other articles.
One should offer oblations with fuel-sticks and clarified butter according to the prescribed rule;
having first sprinkled upwards, one should then perform the downward sprinkling and the general sprinkling.
Three times [one should perform the rite] with water consisting of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) using kuśa grass blades accompanied by the name-mantras;
for that which is not mentioned [here] is stated elsewhere in the Śiva scriptures.
Having thus investigated the application of the limbs, this supreme teacher has fully explained the sequence of mudrās; now listen to the worship of the entire [deity].
O Six-faced One, listen as I shall describe the complete method of propitiation in brief:
it is threefold, namely, the moving, the moving-and-stationary, and the stationary.
That which consists of metal elements is to be known as mobile; that which is made of stone is traditionally held to be both mobile and immobile;
and that which is made of clay, as well as paintings on walls or cloth, is to be known as immobile.

One should worship the deity in those [images]— whether in an earthen one adorned with colors, or on a cloth, or in a mural painting— after first performing the ritual bathing and offering garments and ornaments.
One should cause [the deity] made of iron, solid clay, or painted on cloth or a wall to drink [the offering], along with all the ritual services and the fruits associated with the painting.
One should especially worship him with clay images;
one may perform ritual worship with a stone image, or perform the worship of a gemstone image upon the pedestal of the arms.
The image for ritual worship may extend from the knees to the navel;
however, in the case of a painted image or one made of stone, one should employ metal instead.
If the ritual worship has been performed with the prescribed mantras for one whose worship was previously described,
then one should perform the threefold natural worship there within that ritual worship.
Having taken up the sprinkling water, it is well known that in the work of metalcraft,
[the deity] is placed alone where he is joined by his retinue and the like.
There, one should perform the worship according to the ritual sequence with all the ritual services;
and especially, the images made solely of clarified butter should be installed.
The wise one should perform the sacrifice even without a retinue and so forth;
having then performed the purification of the image according to its essential nature, as derived from the [root] image.
Then, having removed the garland worshipped during all the junctions (sandhyās) from the heart,
one should thoroughly purify the image made of clay, or that which is joined with the seat of the face.
The wise one should purify the *chatra* and the *hāsa* with *kuśa* grass,
or likewise with water as previously described, provided it is used alone.
Gold dust from the night [of the new moon], silver, and salt, when placed in a copper vessel, bring about prosperity; one is purified by the ashes from the hand.
Likewise, metal images should be bathed on every festival day;
for a metal image, a daily bath is not required, but it must be bathed on every festival day.
Having placed a flower upon his head, the preceptor should arrange two seats;
he should then assign Dharma and the other [virtues] to the corners, having mentally projected the feet of the seat.
One should sequentially assign Adharma and the others, as well as the entire set beginning with Cakra;
having covered them with the three qualities (guṇas), one should worship Hari in the center.
Above that, having placed a kalama-vessel with eight petals and a pericarp,
one should install within its center the Deity composed of thirty-eight kalās.
Whatever rite is joined with action, from that one should commence either the ritual worship or the rite;
one should invoke the deity with the *sadyojāta* mantra and perform the placement (*nyāsa*) with the *guhyaka* mantra.
One should effect the complete cessation with the Aghora mantra and the presence with the Puruṣa mantra;
then, with the Hṛdaya mantra, one should offer the arghya water upon the head.
One should cause the water for the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācamana), and the respectful offering (arghya) to be given with the Heart-mantra;
furthermore, the consecration (abhiṣecana) should be performed with the five Brahmans and the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).
The wise one should sprinkle [the vessel] with water from the kuśa grass using the eightfold terrible mantra of Anādṛya;
thereafter, he should present the ornaments, the sacred thread, and the mirror.
The foot should be offered with Īśāna; one should cause it to be given with Sadyojāta.
One should offer the garland with the head-mantra (Śiras) and the incense with Tatpuruṣa.
One should indeed join Dīpa with the Netra-mantra, and Gaurī with the Vāma-mantra;
Gaṅgā in the eastern direction, and Vināyaka in the south.
The commander-in-chief, however, should gradually sip lukewarm water from other vessels;
he should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented with the mantra beginning "devasya tvā."
Having offered water for sipping from the heart-mantra, one should discard the used floral offering;
the wise one should then cause betel-leaf, provided with mouth-perfumes, to be given.
The complete method of worship has been declared, beginning with the *praṇava*; now hear of the seer (*ṛṣi*).
For the *oṃkāra*, the seers are the gods beginning with Brahmā, ending with Svarodanta;
the meter (*chandas*) is the goddess Gāyatrī, and the deity (*devatā*) is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
For the Sadyojāta mantra, Brahman is the presiding deity;
Gāyatrī is said to be the meter, and Gotama is indeed the seer.
Viṣṇu is the presiding deity of the Vāmadeva mantra;
its meter is Anuṣṭubh, its ritual application is as prescribed, and Atri is likewise its seer among the sages.
The Rudras, in the form of the Aghora mantra, are the presiding deities there;
Triṣṭubh is said to be the metre, and Savāmitra is likewise the seer.
The presiding deities of the Puruṣa-mantra are Maheśa and his consort;
Bṛhaspati is said to be the metre, and Śātāla is the Ṛṣi.
The form of the mantra is Īśāna, and Śiva is the presiding deity therein;
Jagatī is said to be the meter, and Bhāradvāja is likewise the seer.
The form known as Sādākhyā is likewise composed of the five Brahmans.
Now I shall explain specifically the procedure for the daily festival; listen.
Made of gold, silver, or copper, it is called a *karaka*;

Having thus taken up the vessel to the north of the pavilion,

The lowest is known as *annaliṅgaka*, performed twice a day;

Furthermore, this is proclaimed as the supreme *liṅga* for all three times;
