She should display the weapon-mudrā as well as the one called the salutation;
Ugrendrā, for the sake of the Lord of the Seers, should worship Induśekharā.
The deity stands upright, joined with a black axe;
his hands grant boons and fearlessness, and he is adorned with a crown of matted hair.
Wearing an island as his garment, with a gentle gaze and a smiling face,
he is the embodiment of the Moon-crested Lord (Śiva) or likewise the embodiment of the Weapon (Astra).
One may worship the form of the image, or otherwise, the linga; or one may perform the propitiation of the sandals. Listen briefly, O Six-faced One.
One should worship the sandals with the Vṛṣadaivatyam hymn and with the mantra of the Bull (Vṛṣa);
having likewise worshipped the world-protectors (Lokapālas) and the image of the sandals.
All ritual services are performed with the Vṛṣagāyatrī mantra;
likewise, in cases of drought, quarrels, binding, and wind-related afflictions, one should act in this manner.
Furthermore, having worshipped the Lingas of the kings of weapons,
one should offer oblations one hundred and eight times with the Pāśupata Heart-mantra.
Having summoned his two attendants, he [appeared] wearing a turban and an upper garment,
endowed with all auspicious marks, and adorned with every ornament.
With the sacred grass (pavitra) held in his hand, he should place the liṅga and especially the image upon the heads of both, having adorned them with perfumes and garlands.
It was provided with canopies and umbrellas, accompanied by fly-whisks,
endowed with all kinds of musical instruments, and filled with dancing and singing.
Adorned with various lamps and attended by various devotees,
it brings delight to Brahmā in the forenoon and to the form of Śiva at midday.
One who desires the bull's favor should circumambulate it three times at night;
one should lead it before the army, upon its head, and likewise within it at the conclusion.
Having first performed a circumambulation accompanied by rhythmic clapping (*tāla*) as Bhṛṅgiṇī,
one should then perform a second circumambulation with the retinue.
The Vṛṣatāla belongs to Vṛṣa, and likewise the Bhṛṅgiṇī to Agni;
the Jharjharī instrument belongs to the Mothers, while the Kekarī belongs to Vighneśa.
In Jyeṣṭhā, there is a pot for Ṣaṇmukha, as well as one with curled locks;
in Taṭaprahāra there is Durgā, and in Caṇḍaka there is Viṣama-antya.
In ancient times, the Śrīkāmarasauvana [region] was bound by the Gāndhāra [scale], the Svara [note], the Vaṇa [note], and the Kauśika [raga],
accompanied by the Bhṛṅgī-pañcama and Mallatāla [rhythms].
Having taken [the image] together with the *keśī*, the *vilita*, and the *ālaya*, accompanied by the sound of musical instruments and the resonance of conchs at the great gate (*gopura*),
he should then perform three circumambulations around the pedestal situated in front.
The abode of all the gods, especially the sacrificial altar (balipīṭha),
is like a supreme lord seeking power over the three worlds— Bhūr, Bhuvar, and Svar.
It is said by the great seers that Bali, which bestows strength upon all beings— especially among humans and the moving and unmoving— is the giver of strength.
For the purpose of circumambulating the three worlds, one performs the circumambulation of the abode of Śiva;
first is the circumambulation of Bhūḥ, and second is the circumambulation of Bhuvaḥ.
The third circumambulation, performed clockwise with beautiful locks of hair, yields great fruit;
Śiva is the auspicious protector of the earth, the intermediate space, and the heavens.
The Ālaya is known as the root-support of all the gods;
performing circumambulation of Śambhu for the sake of protecting the world, [he]—
It is to be constantly resorted to for the sake of Śiva by gods, dānavas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, sages, perfected beings (siddhas), and celestial minstrels (cāraṇas).
The sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) of the great ones is then supported by the deities; it is used during the times of the circumambulation of offerings and in the worship of the retinue.
While performing the three circumambulations, one should avoid stepping on the shadows;
then, having entered inside the Śambara and the pedestal of Bali (balipīṭha).
For Indra, the rhythm should be *samatala*, while for Agni it is *baddhāvaṇa*;
for Yama it is *bhṛṅgiṇītāla*, and for Nairṛti it is *mallatālaka*.
In the west (vāruṇī) is Navatāla; in the northwest (vāyavyā) is Calitālaka;
in the north (saumye) is that which is called Kauśikī; and likewise in the northeast (īśānī) is Ḍhakarī.
The *baliliṅga* should be fashioned according to the previously mentioned procedure;
then, having performed a circumambulation, one should enter the temple.
Taking your stand at the doorway, perform the washing of your feet;
afterwards, enter the abode, having first placed [the water] before the preceptor.
Having taken up the deity from the *liṅga*, one should install the root *liṅga*;
then, one should cause the blow to be given to Caṇḍa with the Caṇḍa-mantra.
Then, hearing the sound of the bali-offering music, the piśācas and brahmarākṣasas went outside the village; [thereby] it bestows an abundance of wealth and grain.
Having thus performed the perpetual festival, the characteristic of the recitation (*japa*) is stated:
O fair-faced one, each single [recitation] is counted by means of a finger.
One should know that a *rekhā* yields eightfold merit, a *putradīpa* tenfold,
a conch shell a hundredfold, and coral a thousandfold.
With crystal beads, ten thousand [repetitions] are performed; with pearls, it is said to be one hundred thousand;
with lotus seeds, one million; and with gold, ten million is said to be accomplished.
By constantly reciting the mantra ten billion times on a *kuśa*-grass knot,
or indeed by reciting it on a sacred *rudrākṣa* bead, a person obtains infinite merit-bestowing fruit.
One should know that the rudrākṣa is the very essence of recitation; there is no counting of the recitation.
When joined with the recitation, it brings about success; thereafter, one should perform the hymn and the mantra.

One should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the *Vyomavyāpin*, the *Tryambaka*, and the five Brahmans along with the six ancillaries (*ṣaḍaṅga*) according to one's capacity, and circumambulate [the deity] three times.
According to the authority stated by Bharata, the *tāṇḍava* and the *geyaka* have been described; the characteristics of *japa* have also been explained. Now listen to the *culukodaka*.
The recitation performed in secret and other such places, protected by secrecy, has been undertaken;
may accomplishment be mine through this, by your grace, O Lord.
Whatever action I have ever performed, whether good or evil, O Śiva, enjoy that for me; O Śaṅkara, consume it.
Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the devotee, and Śiva is this entire world;
Śiva performs sacrifice everywhere—may I become exactly like him.
The wise one, having formed the añjali gesture with the right hand bent at four finger-breadths,
should take a flower or water and cause the youngest [disciple] to hear it.
This is declared to be the water for the hollowed palms; one should offer it to one's own self at the lotus of the feet.
Starting from the heart, [the recitation continues] until the rising of the sun.
A watch (yāma) is said to consist of seven and a half ghaṭikās; this is called "attainment" (siddhi).
Sixty breaths constitute one prāṇa, and sixty of those [prāṇas] make one ghaṭikā.
Sixty *ghaṭikās* constitute a day and night, which is said to have eight junctions (*saṃdhyā*).
That worship performed at the eight junctions is the most excellent of all worships.
The worship for the rite of the maiden should be performed with seven, six, five, four, three, two, or one [verses], according to the three categories beginning with the highest.
One should perform the commencement of worship ending with the dance and the offering of the twilight (sandhyā-pradānaka);
however, if the mind is focused, there is no fault even if one deviates from the sequence beginning with the twilight rite.
What is proclaimed as the procedure for the worship of the Guru’s sandals? Regarding the minor services and the twilight rites, one incurs no fault even if they are deficient.
Just as there is a birth-channel at the time of birth,
so too one should perform worship for one's own sake according to one's capacity and in accordance with the rules.
Bathing should take two ghaṭikās, worship one ghaṭikā,
the offering of food (naivedya) half a ghaṭikā, and the presentation of the bali-oblation should be equal to that.

The daily fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) lasts for half [of that time], the daily festival (*nityotsava*) for two *nāḍikās*, and the *tāṇḍava* dance shall last for one *nāḍī*; one should properly join these with each *saṃdhyā*.
Beginning from sunrise until ten nāḍikās have passed, this is declared to be the morning time (prātaḥkāla); this is called the forenoon (pūrvāhṇa).
Starting from the end of the forenoon until ten nāḍīs [have passed], it should be known as midday; that which follows is called the afternoon here.
Starting from midday until ten nāḍikās have passed, this should be known as the afternoon;
the time following this is called evening.

Beginning from sunset, two *nāḍikās* that have been brought forth should be known as *pradoṣa*; listen now to the half-*yāma* following that. Beginning from the end of *pradoṣa*, three *nāḍikās* consisting of three quarters [of a *yāma*] [constitute it].
This is declared to be half a watch (ardhayāma), and here it is called midnight;
that half-watch begins from that point and lasts for ten nāḍikās.
This is declared to be midnight; it is said here to be the end of the night, occurring three nāḍīs before sunrise, consisting of three quarters.
This is declared to be the end of the night; knowing this, one should perform everything accordingly.
The collection of water, the gathering of flowers, as well as the ritual worship—whatever must be done should be performed at the end of the night, or one may collect the water at that time.
One should perform the installation of the deity and the pilgrimage at the sacred ford during the morning time,
beginning from the early morning until the Kāśika nāḍikā.
To that extent, one should perform the preparatory rites for the sacred site;
indeed, the entire process of offering the ritual sprouts constitutes the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the festival.
At evening, the wise one should begin the binding of the protective thread (rakṣāsūtra),
as well as during the installation, the sprinkling with water (prokṣaṇa), and likewise during the laying of the foundation (garbhanyāsa).
One should perform everything beginning with the formal acceptance (*adhivāsa*), as well as the auspicious rites (*kautuka*),
for the purpose of pleasing all the gods.
One should perform the "Five Great Sounds" (pañcamahāśabda) to avert inauspiciousness;
however, in the case of a palace with a western entrance, there is a slight difference in the ritual worship of Śiva.
One should worship Nandīśa and Narmadā on the right side of the door,
and one should worship Vijaya and Sindhu on the left side of the door.
One should visualize Nandi and the other gatekeepers as before;
having worshipped Vṛṣabha in the west, one should worship Skanda in the east.
One should worship the retinue there, as well as Vṛṣa and Vighneśvara;
one should cause all the ritual services (upacāras) to be offered at the face of Sadyojāta.
One should visualize the seat, the coverings, and so forth as before;
thus has Śiva been worshipped during the twilight rite for one's own sake and for the sake of others.
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who makes an offering even when unable [to do much]:
it increases grain, brings fame, increases longevity, and increases nourishment.
It bestows liberation unseen, grants the fruit of all gifts and sacrifices,
and having uplifted twenty-one generations of one's lineage, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
What indeed can be done for Śiva, who is perfectly complete, by people?
Whatever is done for the devotees of Śiva, that is considered as having been done for Śiva himself.
[Thus ends the chapter on daily worship in the Vātula-tantra, the Thousandfold Compendium.]
Hariḥ Om.
